Even when a person feels cast into spiritual exile and distance, the moment he turns his whole heart to seek the Blessed Name from that very place, he discovers that God is closer to him than ever.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And from the phrase "like a son who searches," it is evident that through this attained knowledge he is crowned a son, resembling one exploring inner treasures; proving that specific knowledge refers to the inner mysteries of the Torah, except that at Sinai, hearing the commandments directly from the Almighty, they attained prophetic stature and perceived for that singular moment the esoteric Work of the Chariot, wherefore Scripture used the singular "your God"; whereas the perpetual commandment of "I am" for subsequent generations, which omits "this day" and binds all Jews, commands general faith.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “I remember for you the devotion of your youth, the love of your espousals, how you walked after Me in the wilderness, in an unsown land” (Jeremiah 2:2). When a person stands in serene clarity of mind, it is easy to recognize that God governs all; the true test and preciousness of Israel’s service is when a person’s mind is constricted in the ‘unsown wilderness’ of confusion, yet he continues to walk loyally after the Blessed Name.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And in non-leap years we read Parashat Shemini immediately after Passover, wherein it is stated: "These are the living creatures which you may eat..." [Leviticus 11:2], for this passage likewise instructs disciplined boundaries regarding eating; and through the sanctified eating of matzah, one merits subsequently to clarify and purge the evil mixed within eating, for through being consecrated in positive holiness one subsequently merits sifting out the evil, parallel to "I am Hashem your God" being immediately followed by "You shall have no other gods."
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And so unfolded the second Tablets (Zohar Va'etchanan 261a): in the first Tablets the commandments were without a Vav and shattered; while in the second Tablets all are inscribed with a Vav: “And you shall not murder,” “and you shall not commit adultery,” etc., and therefore they endured. For both share one root (Zohar Vayikra 11b: Ten Utterances of Genesis and Ten of Sinai): from mortal intellect the commandments appear conflicting: murder being the dross of Gevurah, adultery the dross of Chesed.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Only that at the sin of the Golden Calf the defect returned through the drive for idolatry—the opposite extreme—wherein they sought to flee physical appetites so excessively that they demanded "gods that shall go before us", which Onkelos rendered as dachlan (objects of dread), seeking external dread to fence their desires, which caused them to relapse; therefore the Sages expounded: "Let the mother [the cow] come and wipe up the excrement of her calf", for the red heifer also atones for the Golden Calf, since that idolatrous drive was born only as an overreaction to the primal drive of lust, swinging to the morbid opposite extreme.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Re'eh 6:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “When God shall enlarge your borders … and you will say, ‘I shall eat meat’ … you shall eat meat according to the desire of your soul .…” (Devarim, 12:20)It is not said that they will go outside of their borders, but only that their borders will become enlarged. In truth, God’s name, Hava’ye (YHVH, called the Tetragrammaton) signifies that from God’s perspective He has chosen Israel, He has no borders, and thus He permits one to extend freely in all the goodness that God gives.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Pirkei Avot 4:2: ‘Ben Azzai said: Be quick in performing a minor commandment as in the case of a major one, and flee from transgression; For one commandment leads to another commandment, and transgression leads to another transgression; For the reward for performing a commandment is another commandment and the reward for committing a transgression is a transgression.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:66, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Pirkei Avot 4:2) to illuminate his teaching here (““The retribution of a transgression is another transgression” Avot 4:2, in the manner of the Sages Shabbat 105b: Such is the way of the evil inclination: today it says to him do this, etc., and “one transgression...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.

And though in holiness the primary sanctification is required for the material body and animal soul; whereas the supernal soul is emanated from a holy realm and is intrinsically holy; nevertheless, it descended into a physical body in this world specifically that it might ascend far higher than its original state if it purifies its path.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And behold, the two attributes “one who does not become angry” and “one who does not become intoxicated” correspond to “You shall not murder” and “You shall not commit adultery,” as in Yoma (75a): “Whoever fixes his eyes upon his cup, all forbidden relationships appear to him like a plain”; and though anger and lust appear as polar opposites, at the root they are one, akin to the impulse for idolatry, as in Avodah Zarah (17a): “Regarding the impulse to transgression, once one is deeply attached to it, it resembles heresy.”

(Beit Yaakov, Bereishit, Vayeira 1:2).

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And we battle incessantly against it, and Hashem will not abandon man into its hand, – and to this alludes 'You have shielded my head in the day of weapons'— meaning on the day of struggle against it. And it is designated 'a covenant of fire,' because whoever walks after the lust of his heart is condemned to the fire of Gehenna, as they taught (Pirkei Avot 4:2): 'and the consequence of a sin is a sin,' meaning that out of the very transgression itself the fire of Gehenna is forged.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 28b: ‘After mentioning until when the additional prayer may be recited, the Gemara relates: Rav Avya was ill and did not come to Rav Yosef’s Shabbat lecture. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And these correspond to the two prayers of Rabbi Nechuniah ben HaKanah upon entering the study hall and upon leaving it (Berakhot 28b) see there: the entrance prayer contains 123 letters, three less than three times the 42-letter Name; while the exit prayer contains 213 letters, three less than three times the 72-letter Name; for in truth he would weave the Name of Adonut together with Havayah, binding himself to the Master of the world, and this is not the place to lengthen.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 54a: ‘The mishna articulates a general principle: One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him, as it is stated: “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5). Alternatively, it may…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:67, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 54a) to illuminate his teaching here (“And it appears that Maimonides was troubled by the formulation of Ben Azzai, who stated: “One offers thanksgiving for the past and cries out in supplication for the future” Berakhot 54a; for ostensibly the reverse...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And regarding this the mitzvah of love says “with all your soul,” whose plain sense is, as they said, to give over one’s very life and soul for the love of Hashem; and it prefaced “with all your heart,” which the Sages expounded [Berachos 54a] “with your two inclinations” — for this too is of the middah of love., the good inclination and the evil inclination; ‘with all your soul’ — even if He takes your soul; ‘with all your might [me’odecha]’ — with all your money; another interpretation: with every measure [middah] He metes out to you, thank Him exceedingly.”

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5)—even if He takes your soul: Rabbi Akiva rejoiced at the hour of his martyrdom because throughout his life he longed to fulfill the verse literally, teaching that when a person surrenders every trace of personal agenda to the Blessed Name, even the darkest trial reveals the innermost point of love in the heart.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 13:16: ‘These are the names of the men whom Moses sent to scout the land; but Moses changed the name of Hosea son of Nun to Joshua.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:68, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 13:16) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is the rendering of Targum Yonatan Numbers 13:16: When Moses saw the intense humility of Joshua, Moses called Hoshea son of Nun “Joshua”; matching the homily of the Sages Sotah 34b: “May God Yah save you...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And it is known from the Arizal that wherever a letter of the Name Havayah is added, there is in it an augmentation of spiritual elevation and sanctity, and all the more so the letter vav, which is the sign of Truth, as stated (in the Zohar, start of Vayikra 2a). And this is [the meaning of] avon spelled fully: that even [a trace of bodily pleasure touches] one who cleaves to Truth completely; and this is the rung of Yaakov, who “did not die” (Taanis 5b), for death stems from falsehood, which endures only for a moment and has no permanence (Mishlei 12:19).

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “For the Lord your God is in your midst, a great and awesome God” (Deuteronomy 7:21). The Gemara in Berakhot 33a declares: “Great is knowledge (de’ah), for it was placed between two Divine Names.” When a person sanctifies his mind and even his physical eating with da’at—recognizing that every sustainment flows from the Blessed Name in his midst—all his faculties are drawn into holiness.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sotah 34b: ‘The Gemara explains: Joshua did not go to the graves of the forefathers because Moses had already prayed for mercy for him, as it is stated: “And Moses called Hoshea son of Nun Joshua [Yehoshua]” (Numbers 13:16), meaning: God will save you [Ya yoshiakha] from the counsel of the spies. And this is the meaning of that which is written: “But My servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and has followed Me fully, him will I bring into the land where into he went” (Numbers 14:24), which implies that Caleb changed his mind over time. Joshua, however, was opposed to the intentions of the other spies from the outset.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:68, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 34b) to illuminate his teaching here (“matching the homily of the Sages Sotah 34b: “May God Yah save you from the counsel of the spies,” that he not bow before their intimidation out of excessive modesty:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And there are deeper matters within this, for the aforementioned teaching mirrors the Talmudic statement in Avodah Zarah 5a: "Had our ancestors not sinned, we would be as though we had never come into the world." And we will likewise explain why Moses renamed him "Joshua" at the dispatching of the spies, saying: "May God save you from the counsel of the spies," as expounded by our Sages (Sotah 34b), and why he did not pray for all of them as well.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Re'eh 2
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “See! I give before you today a blessing and a curse.” (Devarim, 11:26)This means that each time the Holy One, blessed be He, bestows goodness to man, He dresses it in a garment where it appears on the outside to be the opposite from that goodness. (This is explained in the Mei HaShiloach in Parshat Korach, on the verse, “and I put my word in his mouth.”) In this way man may refine himself by his actions and bring to light the goodness that is at the depths.

For they spoke no empty falsehood in declaring "it is a land that eats up its inhabitants" Numbers 13:32, having foreseen future destructions and exiles, which were preordained from the Six Days of Creation (Bereishit Rabbah 2:4).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Talmud, Shabbat 21b:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: In the laws of Shabbat, the sukkah represents the sanctification of place, whereas the mavoy (alleyway) represents the sanctification of time, for the choicest of all times is Shabbat. And regarding the Chanukah lamp placed below twenty cubits: the light of Chanukah illuminates even when a person feels himself in a lowly state below higher spiritual comprehension, shining the light of Divine providence into the public thoroughfare.

And in the Zohar (Shelach 158a): this refers to the Tree of Life (Etz Chaim), as written: "a desire fulfilled is a tree of life" (Proverbs 13:12), showing that for physical desire the true healing is the Tree of Life.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:18–19

And upon such a holy union Hashem watches continually to bestow good upon them all the days. And for this reason in the Land of Israel, concerning which it is written (I Kings 9:3): "and Mine eyes and Mine heart shall be there perpetually", continuously without any separation, therefore the fruits of the Land of Israel in its inhabited state were bestowed with an exceedingly generous eye.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: II Kings 2:19: ‘The leaders of the town said to Elisha, “Look, the town is a pleasant place to live in, as my lord can see; but the water is bad and the land causes bereavement.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:70, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (II Kings 2:19) to illuminate his teaching here (““And what the land is that they dwell in” Numbers 13:19—referring to inhabited settlements, whether the cities are salubrious for human habitation, as in the narrative of Elisha II Kings 2:19; whereas “and what the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this follows the dictum (Avodah Zarah 19a): initially it is called "the Torah of Hashem," but ultimately "his own Torah," which is the mystery of the Written and Oral Torahs across all levels. And the rung of Samuel, weighed equally against Moses and Aaron who root the Written Torah, marks the inception of this level termed "the Torah of Hashem," for he was preordained thus from birth, a heavenly voice heralding him prior to his conception; while Habakkuk the son of the Shunammite represents the culmination at the zenith of prophetic expansion in the days of Elisha, who inherited a double portion of Elijah's spirit [II Kings 2:9].
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Mei HaShiloach Anthology, Talmud, Sukkah 51a
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: At the Rejoicing of the Place of the Water-Drawing (Simchat Beit HaSho’evah), whoever did not see that joy never saw true joy in his days: for water symbolizes the primordial, colorless flow of supernal wisdom prior to any constriction, and drawing water with joy awakens the holy spirit (ruach ha-kodesh) and the complete refinement of the heart.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 13:20: ‘Is the soil rich or poor? Is it wooded or not? Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: He, whose soul encompassed them, encompassing the entire fruit of the Torah as well. Therefore he sent spies, the Sages expounding (Sotah 34b): "Send for yourself" Numbers 13:2—according to your own judgment, I do not command you; for sending spies is a natural military strategy pursued by earthly kings; whereas for the wilderness generation whose entire existence was completely supernatural, what need was there for spies?
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree.” Behold, just as a distinction exists between grass and herbs—which endure merely for a single season and not permanently— and trees, which possess lasting permanence from being firmly planted initially, whereupon the sap continually ascends to nourish them, and they reproduce perpetually from their seed sown in the soil without ever ceasing— so is the reality within the human realm: the wicked endure only temporarily like fleeting grass, whereas Israel possesses eternal endurance like deep-rooted trees.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 13:20: ‘Is the soil rich or poor? Is it wooded or not? And take pains to bring back some of the fruit of the land.”—Now it happened to be the season of the first ripe grapes.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:70, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 13:20) to illuminate his teaching here (““whether there is wood therein” ibid.—for sweet fruits flourish in warm climates while robust timber grows in cold climates, and the Land of Israel uniquely integrates both virtues:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Egypt bordering the Holy Land which possesses all things in holiness through the Torah; for "there is no wisdom like the wisdom of the Land of Israel" (Bereishis Rabbah 16:4); and so in might, the Spies reporting "the people is strong," the Land raising heroes in holiness; as it is said: "And five of you shall chase a hundred, and a hundred of you shall put ten thousand to flight" (Vayikra 26:8); but within Israel this occurs through the Torah; as Rashi expounds from Sifra: many performing a mitzvah possess exponential strength.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Exodus, Tetzaveh 1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And you will command the children of Israel … take unto yourself pure olive oil ….” (Shemot, 27:20)“Unto yourself,” meaning to the Chochma (wisdom) inherent in every soul of Israel, and all the wisdom of Israel is called in the name of Moshe Rabeynu. To this God commanded that every one of Israel shall take to the wisdom inside of him some pure olive oil, meaning refined wisdom, and that is that he should not turn to any side that might be tainted.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Psalms 121:5: ‘GOD is your guardian, GOD is your protectionat your right hand.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:71, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Psalms 121:5) to illuminate his teaching here (““Hashem is your shadow” Psalms 121:5: a shadow progressively shortens until solar midday when it contracts to its minimum, and thereafter reverses and lengthens steadily; so too Israel: when they descend to the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And ostensibly, what kind of authenticating sign is this? Since it was passed down thus, everyone knew of this tradition, and certainly anyone who would come and boast that he will redeem them would state the wording matching the tradition, so what was the point of the sign?! But in truth it is known from our Sages on "Hashem is your shadow" [Psalms 121:5], that He acts like a shadow reflecting whatever the body does, all His attributes operating measure for measure, not arbitrarily, but because mortals visit and remember Him as well.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: ‘Drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved’ (Song of Songs 5:1)—these are below, termed ‘beloved’ (dodim) at designated appointed times, as we have established.” And to this also alludes the Zohar (Naso 129a): The eyes of the White Head (Arich Anpin), etc.; Rabbi Shimon asked Rabbi Abba: To what does this allude? He replied: To the fish of the sea who have no eyelids covering their eyes, never sleeping; this is what is written (Psalms 121:4): “Behold, He that keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 14:9: ‘only you must not rebel against GOD. Have no fear then of the people of the country, for they are our prey: their protection has departed from them, but GOD is with us. Have no fear of them!”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:71, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 14:9) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is: “their defense tzillam, their shadow is removed from them” Numbers 14:9—the nations decline until total eclipse without ever re-extending their shadow. Or it may be explained according to the tradition...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: But the Ma'apilim did not succeed in this because they ate it unripe, as our Sages stated (Sotah 49b): "In the footsteps of the Messiah audacity will increase," for only then is the proper hour for this and in the future: "A woman shall court a man" (Jeremiah 31:21), and this is not the place to elaborate. And therefore Moses said to them: "And it shall not prosper" (Numbers 14:41)— indicating that it is a valid concept, only that it would not prosper at that time; and he was precise in saying "and it" (ve-hi)—for everywhere our Sages expound: "it, but not another,"
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it.” It is stated in Midrash Rabbah (Bereishit 11:2): He blessed it with the manna and sanctified it with the manna. The meaning is: on Shabbat the Blessed Name constricts man, granting no room for autonomous physical activity; for even though during the six workdays Hashem remains the sole ultimate Actor and Sustainer, the distinction is this: during the six workdays man is granted license to assist Him (as it were), fulfilling “And now, let the power of the Lord be great” (Numbers 14:17) and the Gemara (Shabbat 89a): “You should have helped Me”.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Zohar, Terumah 29:288-296: ‘And had the eye but the power and permission to perceive such matters, it would behold on the nights of Sabbaths, New Moons, and festivals, a kind of figures singing and praising the Holy One above their graves. But the folly of the children of men prevents them from having any cognizance of these matters, since they neither know nor perceive what the foundation of their lives in the world is, and have no mind to be aware of the glory of the Supernal King in this world which they can see, not to speak of the world to come, which they see not; thus they have no perception of the basis of either, or of the inner meaning of these things.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:71, Rav Tzadok draws upon this kabbalistic teaching (Zohar, Terumah 29:288-296) to illuminate his teaching here (“Or it may be explained according to the tradition to examine one's shadow on Hoshana Rabbah, thirty days prior to death the shadow withdrawing Zohar II, 142a. “they are bread for us” ibid.—this refers to the milk and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Only when it is carried out in holiness according to human capacity for the Holy One does not act tyrannically, and our Sages noted: "in total iniquity"—meaning even the most pious of the pious cannot entirely avoid some subtle base element (Midrash Rabbah, Tazria 14:5), then "Hashem is your shadow" (Psalms 121:5): a corresponding holy influx is poured out unto the Supernal Earth (Malchut), which had been made barren and parched through his past sins, as brought in the Tikkunim, and everything is healed.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Nitzavim 1:3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: This perplexed King Shlomo, and he said (Mishlei, 30:18), “three things are beyond me, and four I did not know … the way of man with woman.” This means the choicest elements in Israel, like the one who completes God’s will, and in this way, “with the young woman [b’almah],” meaning it is so also with the meekest of Israel. This is the explanation of “You are standing.”

Have no fear then of the people of the country, for they are our prey: their protection has departed from them, but GOD is with us. Have no fear of them!”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:71, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 14:9) to illuminate his teaching here (““they are bread for us” ibid.—this refers to the milk and honey of the Land: it is our bread and we shall consume it, fearing not that the inhabitants of the land will withhold it:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Which had not been the case previously at the Exodus from Egypt, where although it was a far greater supernatural salvation, there was nonetheless a "great protest against the Torah" (Shabbos 88a); for then the miracle was one of passive open revelation of the Shechinah, and when that revelation withdrew everything vanished, until they said: "Let us appoint a captain, and let us return into Egypt" (Bamidbar 14:4); for once that revelation which they experienced at the Exodus withdrew, they thought to return to Egypt.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Balak 1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And Balak saw .…” (Bamidbar, 22:1)This Parsha is written in the Torah because “He showed His people the power of His actions to give them the inheritance of the nations” (Tehilim, 111:6). Here God showed Moshe in a prophetic message what Balak was thinking and how he feared Israel. Also concerning Rachav (Joshua, Ch. 2), when Israel saw that fear of them had spread over the nations, they then understood that God is giving them the land as an inheritance.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 14:20: ‘And GOD said, “I pardon, as you have asked.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:72, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 14:20) to illuminate his teaching here (““I have pardoned according to your word” Numbers 14:20—yet strictly “according to your word,” as you stated: “and as You have forgiven this people, from Egypt even until now” ibid. 14:19, alluding to the Golden Calf,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And with a gift, where he may acquire that which does not belong to his soul, his life-force is forced to expand into an alien vessel, whereby his vitality can be diminished! The theme: Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah’s longevity, measure for measure in unearned years, and how years are shortened. In Megillah (28a), Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKanah was asked by his disciples: "In what merit have you prolonged your days?" He answered: "In all my days I never accepted gifts, and I was forgiving of my money". The eunuchs (gavzei) struck the questioner, knowing that Rabbi Nechunya’s longevity was his allotted lifespan and that he had never sinned to have it curtailed.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Numbers, Bamidbar 5:2
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: This way, if he hears something improper, he can close his ears with his fingers.” Therefore when they descended into the impure air of Egypt, they went by the name Etsbon (like finger), for they would close their ears in order not to receive anything that was not God’s will. Then when they entered the land of Israel, where the air is filled with Kedusha, they were called “Izni [whch means ear],”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 14:21: “‘But in very deed, as I live—and all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord—’” Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:72, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 14:21) to illuminate his teaching here (“so now too He did not destroy them immediately, yet decreed: “But as truly as I live...” ibid. 14:21, exacting retribution incrementally over forty years. “and all the earth shall be filled with the glory of Hashem”...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: “And then all the rungs of teshuvah and its heights will be revealed in expansive, actual revelation; and from the rung of the ‘lengthening of years’ we will merit ‘and we shall live’” (cf. Hoshea 6:2)” — “He will revive us after two days; on the third day He will raise us up, and we shall live before Him.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — a prophecy of Israel’s future revival and resurrection. R’ Tzadok’s use: from the rung of a mere “lengthening of years,” Israel will ascend to “and we shall live” — the full life of the days of Mashiach and the World to Come.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And as my revered grandfather explained: “I will make him a helper opposite/against him (ezer kenegdo)” — within creation, every true assistance emerges specifically from that which opposes it; that is, Hashem placed before man all manner of obstacles, and man progressively expands Heavenly glory, dissolves all the obstacles, and redirects everything face-to-face to Hashem — and then man realizes that from these very obstacles came his greatest divine support.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 14:21: “‘But in very deed, as I live—and all the earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord—’” Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:72, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 14:21) to illuminate his teaching here (““and all the earth shall be filled with the glory of Hashem” ibid.—is a parenthetical clause, the thought continuing: “As I live, surely all those men...” ibid. 14:21–22; answering Moses’ plea lest the nations say...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And when he remembers his ultimate end—that all will dissolve into chaos, that everything is vanity and deceitful bread, and afterwards his mouth will be filled with gravel, and nothing remains to man from those vanities except what he exerted toward the service of Hashem— then his uncircumcised heart will at least be humbled; when he takes to heart and contemplates deeply his inevitable demise, his final destiny, and how close he is to shattering, then the ship's captain (rav hachovel) will surely awaken—meaning the foremost governor of the body, which is the innermost will of the heart.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Lech Lecha 1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: "And Avram was very heavy" (Genesis 13:2). An expression of burdensome heaviness, for it felt like a burdensome bother to him, as though saying: Why do I require such overwhelming wealth?! And this explains what Hashem, blessed be He, said to him after Lot separated from him: (Genesis 13:17) – "Arise, walk through the land in the length of it and in the breadth of it; for unto you will I give it"— that He would grant him expansive space in holiness to extend forth, to demonstrate that from all his physical possessions honor of Heaven would result.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 14:22: “‘Surely all those men who have seen My glory, and My signs, which I wrought in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have put Me to proof these ten times, and have not hearkened to My voice, shall not see the land.’” Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:72, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 14:22) to illuminate his teaching here (““and all the earth shall be filled with the glory of Hashem” ibid.—is a parenthetical clause, the thought continuing: “As I live, surely all those men...” ibid. 14:21–22; answering Moses’ plea lest the nations say...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And both are termed "signs" (simanim), being indicators through which vitality is preserved. And in them the sign of life is recognized, for with declining vitality eating, speech, and voice weaken or cease. And the trachea together with lungs, heart, and liver suspended from it, and the esophagus with digestive organs attached to it, literally mirror soul and body, these ministering to the spiritual traits of the soul, and those to bodily faculties.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Bereshit 3
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And God said: Let there be light, and there was light; and God saw the light that it was good; and God divided the light from the darkness; and God called the light Day, etc. 'Light' is mentioned five times: the first 'Let there be light' is when Hashem prepares within Himself to radiate unto man, while the person does not yet perceive or sense this at all, only Hashem is actively preparing to illuminate man; and afterward 'and there was light'—when man begins to sense it; and following that 'and God saw the light that it was good'— when man recognizes his Creator and understands that it is good to be drawn after Hashem, blessed be He; 'and God divided…

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Numbers 14:16: “‘Because the Lord was not able to bring this people into the land which He swore unto them, therefore He has slain them in the wilderness.’” Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:72, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Numbers 14:16) to illuminate his teaching here (“answering Moses’ plea lest the nations say “Because Hashem was not able” ibid. 14:16, God responding that His glory would nevertheless fill the earth:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Therefore they placed “we will do” before “we will hear,” because they are prepared to do whatever the blessed God commands. For this, the nations called them “an impetuous people,” etc.: “If you are able, accept it,” etc., as stated in the chapter “Rabbi Akiva” (Shabbat 88a). For they thought Israel was like them, with things they were unable to do.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Do not defile your daughter by making her into a whore, do not prostitute the land, and fill it with perversity.” (Vayikra, 19:29)“Your daughter” is like the expression “the pupil [literally, ‘daughter’] of the eye.” The Holy One, blessed be He, is warning us to guard the eye, lest, God forbid, it should bring perversity to the heart, for the land is hinted at in the heart, and “the muscles of the eye are connected to the heart”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Batra 119a: ‘Rabbi Ḥideka continues citing Rabbi Shimon HaShikmoni: And Moses our teacher similarly knew that the wood gatherer, who gathered wood on Shabbat (see Numbers 15:32–36), was to be punished by death, as it is stated: “Every one that profanes it shall be put to death” (Exodus 31:14), but he did not know by which death penalty the wood gatherer must die. And the Torah portion concerning the punishment of the wood gatherer was fit to have been written through God initiating a commandment to Moses, to teach which form of court-imposed capital punishment is administered to one who violates Shabbat. But the wood gatherer was found guilty, and the portion was written through the incident…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:73, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 119a) to illuminate his teaching here (“Bava Batra 119a: Shimon the Shikmonite, a disciple of Rabbi Akiva, taught: Moses knew that the wood-gatherer on the Sabbath was liable to death, etc.; it specifically notes “disciples of Rabbi Akiva,” for Rabbi Akiva...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.

And that is: the northern direction is not fully enclosed (Bava Batra 25b); and Hashem left this corner open to be fenced in, remaining incomplete since Creation; and man completes that direction by fencing it through Hashem's holy service, as brought in the holy Zohar (Korach 178b): “'And the Levite, he shall serve'—he completes the left side.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 96b: ‘It is obvious to Rav Yehuda that one who carries four cubits in the public domain is liable to receive the death penalty. In other words, this Master maintains: With regard to this labor, in any case, there is no uncertainty. And this Master maintains: With regard to that labor, in any case, there is no uncertainty. Each Sage maintains that the prohibited labor that he attributed to the wood gatherer incurs the death penalty and is certainly not the labor referred to in the hidden scroll.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:73, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 96b) to illuminate his teaching here (“it specifically notes “disciples of Rabbi Akiva,” for Rabbi Akiva held in Shabbat 96b that the gatherer was Zelophehad, unconcerned by the rebuke “the Torah concealed his identity and you reveal it,” because he...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: But eating meat is forbidden, permitted only to a Torah scholar; which is why Tractate Chullin was codified within the Order of Kodashim (Holy Things), being sanctioned only for one who partakes of mundane food in the purity of consecrated meat, whose table resembles the altar and whose meat is like a holy sacrifice. And this elevation is possible solely through words of Torah, as stated: since the Temple was destroyed, the Holy One has nothing in His world except the four cubits of Halakhah.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Just as it is related in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 84a): Originally, when Rabbi Yochanan stated a teaching, Reish Lakish would raise twenty-four objections against him, [and Rabbi Yochanan would provide twenty-four resolutions,] and consequently the teaching became vastly clarified and broadened. This illustrates that Hashem determined that all genuine breakthroughs and assistance must emerge specifically through an opposing force; and this is the Rabbinic maxim: “If he merits, it is a helper (ezer); if he does not merit, it is against him (kenegdo).”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 97a: ‘On a similar note, Rabbi Akiva revealed an additional matter not explicitly articulated in the Torah. You say that when Aaron and Miriam spoke against Moses, both Aaron and Miriam were struck with leprosy, as it written: “And God became angry at them and He left, and the cloud departed from above the tent, and behold, Miriam was leprous like snow. And Aaron turned toward Miriam, and behold, she was leprous” (Numbers 12:9–10). The verse’s statement that God became angry at both of them teaches that Aaron, too, became leprous; this is the statement of Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira said to him: Akiva, in either case you will be judged in the future for this teaching. If the truth is…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:73, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 97a) to illuminate his teaching here (“And in Shabbat 97a Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira reprimanded: “Akiva, either way you will have to give an accounting”; meaning: according to Rabbi Akiva’s own position in Makkot 7a no capital execution would ever occur,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Makkot 7a: ‘The mishna teaches that Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say: If we had been members of the Sanhedrin, we would have conducted the trials in a manner where no person would have ever been executed. The Gemara asks: How would they have acted to spare the accused from execution if witnesses testified that he intentionally committed murder? Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar both say that they would have asked the witnesses: Did you see whether the accused killed a tereifa, i.e., a person with a condition that would lead to his death within twelve months, or if he killed someone who was intact? The halakhic status of a tereifa is like that of one who is dead, in the sense that one who kills him is…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:73, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Makkot 7a) to illuminate his teaching here (“meaning: according to Rabbi Akiva’s own position in Makkot 7a no capital execution would ever occur, for in Sabbath desecration the court would cross-examine: perhaps the transgressor was biologically terminally ill...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: But this is not sufficient [reason] — to render “judgment without [true] judgment”; the responsibility for [administering] the penalties is not [ours to force by such logic]. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And Joshua whose face was like the moon (Bava Batra 75a) inaugurated this stage of studying Torah by night; previously there having been only Written Torah and the day-level shining from Moses like the sun, the Torah being titled after him "the Torah of Moses" (Bamidbar Rabbah 12:9); and subsequently began Joshua's moon-face, his Torah making known his deficiencies, lacking Moses' solar light and yearning for it, thereby meriting the day and the strand of grace; wherefore his book opens: "Now it came to pass after the death of Moses" Joshua 1:1.

And within Israel too: 'the Holy One decrees and the righteous nullifies', yet it is truly Hashem's inner desire that the tzaddik nullify it; and as stated to Moses our teacher: 'Let Me alone' (Exodus 32:10).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Batra 75a: ‘Rabba says that Rabbi Yoḥanan says: In the future, the Holy One, Blessed be He, will make a feast for the righteous from the flesh of the leviathan, as it is stated: “The ḥabbarim will make a feast [yikhru] of him” (Job 40:30). And kera means nothing other than a feast, as it is stated: “And he prepared [va’yikhreh] for them a great feast [kera]; and they ate and drank” (II Kings 6:23). And ḥabbarim means nothing other than Torah scholars, as it is stated: “You that dwell in the gardens, the companions [ḥaverim] hearken for your voice: Cause me to hear it” (Song of Songs 8:13). This verse is interpreted as referring to Torah scholars, who listen to God’s voice.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:74, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 75a) to illuminate his teaching here (““The countenance of Joshua was like the face of the moon” ibid.—whose illumination is received from another, waxing and waning; and so Joshua: when Israel stumbled in sin at Ai, he fell on his face before the angel...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And concerning this they taught (Bava Batra 75a): 'The countenance of Joshua was like the face of the moon,' and this reflective aspect is designated 'darkness' and 'night', as they expounded (Sanhedrin 24a): ''He has set me in dark places'—this refers to the Babylonian Talmud.' – And in Tanchuma (Parashat Noach 3) on the verse: ''The people walking in darkness have seen a great light'— this is the great primordial light that the Holy One hid away for those who toil in the Oral Torah.'

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And He said, if you will surely hearken to the voice of Hashem your God.” (Shemot, 15:26)That is to say you will be willing to hear His voice, which is the fulfillment of the mitzvot. (The author explains each phrase in the verse.) “And that which is honest in His eyes you will do”—“honest” means that you will perform His mitzvot with love and affection, and you will understand how to have in mind the awesome depth of God’s consciousness in order to do more than He commanded you.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sanhedrin 11a: ‘§ Since Shmuel HaKatan and his great piety were mentioned, the Gemara now relates several incidents that shed additional light on his personality. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Just as the prophets heard Hashem directly face-to-face, so after prophecy ceased He spoke to them from behind via the reverberating echo. As is known in natural science: when acoustic sound strikes a solid barrier, it rebounds and produces an echo resembling the original voice. And naturalists constructed chambers reflecting sound waves back and forth, the secondary echo sounding like an autonomous voice, though it is merely the rear reflection of the primeval utterance.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And these utterances are an ongoing prophecy for every generation and every individual Jewish soul, to know how Hashem engages with every single soul of Israel. And although the entire Torah constitutes prophetic pathways to understand the engagement Hashem maintains with His people Israel, nonetheless here is Hashem's prophecy revealed most explicitly within the mystery of the Tetragrammaton (Havayah): The first utterance points to the letter Yud of the Name Havayah.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Nedarim 39b: ‘Apropos the conflict between Moses and Korah, the Gemara cites an additional verse that Rava interpreted homiletically, and some say that it was Rabbi Yitzḥak who said: What is the meaning of that which is written: “The sun and moon stood still in their habitation [zevula], at the light of Your arrows as they go, at the shining of Your glittering spear” (Habakkuk 3:11)? Meaning, in its theological depth the failure of the Dispersion was far graver than that of the Flood: for the Dispersion acted with calculated obstinacy to force Hashem's presence to dwell among their impurities, as though waging war and conquering Him (like sorcery that diminishes the heavenly entourage, Chullin 7b)—which is saying to the King: “I and not you.”
