Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And Avraham and Yitzchak too are [retroactively] “called Yaakov,” meaning that once he came into the world, they too were “clarified,” for [in the fullest sense] only Yaakov is called “the seed” of the Avos, as they said in Nedarim. It follows that their “beds,” too, were whole, for the “dross” (Yishmael, Esav) is not their [true] seed at all, since it did not come from their side.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Therefore he must halt midway in whatever affair he stands at the onset of Shabbat, preventing the garment from expanding any further; returning himself to the Root of all garments, so that light may flow into all his weekday deeds, ensuring that his expansive weekday labors remain unblemished. “And feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father” — Our Sages expounded (Shabbat 118a): “An inheritance without boundaries; not like Abraham... but like Jacob concerning whom it is said: ‘And you shall spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south.’”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 28:15: ‘Remember, I am with you: I will protect you wherever you go and will bring you back to this land. I will not leave you until I have done what I have promised you.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:113, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 28:15) to illuminate his teaching here (“but once promised “and I will bring you back into this land” ibid. 28:15, he viewed it merely as an alien land: “the land of the people of the east.” Wherefore “he lifted up his feet” with eager haste; as ruled in...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And our father Jacob, peace be upon him, who is the root of the entire nation of Israel, was promised 'I will not leave you until, etc.' – meaning that the prior illumination would be so powerful that he was guaranteed that even during the subsequent withdrawal the righteous would not be forsaken, and in all that he does he would prosper, for his bed was wholly pure.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 48:3–4
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And in this do the God-fearing choose: that even though they see that all human deeds and plans stem from Hashem, even what is done unconsciously, they on their part do not settle for this, performing their actions with discernment and knowledge wherever they turn. And this is what was promised to him (Genesis 17:8): “to give unto you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan”: for among the nations it is termed merely 'the land of Canaan', since after Hashem showed them that man cannot bypass the divine will, they abandon serving Him.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 6b: ‘Rabbi Ḥelbo said that Rav Huna said: One who leaves the synagogue should not take large strides because it creates the impression that he is eager to leave. Abaye explained Rav Huna’s statement and said: This halakha was only said with regard to leaving the synagogue, where large strides seem particularly disrespectful. However, with regard to entering a synagogue, it is a mitzva to run and one is permitted to rush and take large strides (Rabbi Yoshiyahu Pinto). As it is said: “And let us know, eagerly strive to know the Lord” (Hosea 6:3). One who eagerly enters a synagogue displays his enthusiasm to follow the path of God.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:113, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 6b) to illuminate his teaching here (“Wherefore “he lifted up his feet” with eager haste; as ruled in Berakhot 6b: one must not run when leaving a synagogue lest he appear to cast off a burden, but if he intends to return he may run, hastening to...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For Jacob's rest is "the consummate rest that You desire"; as stated: "the righteous have no rest, neither in this world nor in the World to Come: 'they go from strength to strength' (Tehillim 84:8)" (Berachos 64a); for this is their entire rest: when they are empowered to run after Hashem; wherefore it is a mitzvah to run to a commandment or to words of Torah even on Shabbat (Berachos 6b); and communal sacrifices override Shabbat (Pesachim 66a), their true rest being to serve the Blessed Name in truth.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:31 (§2)
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this is what Hashem, blessed be He, said to him: "And I will make you a great nation," (Genesis 12:2), and the Sages expounded upon this in Midrash Tanchuma (Lech Lecha): "I am making you a new creation," meaning that it is accounted unto him as though he created himself. And the inner concept in this is that the spiritual level of Avraham our Father, peace be upon him, was akin to what they said in the Talmud (Berakhot 6b): "The reward for attending the assembly is the distress of crowding; the reward for the discourse is the running to hear it,"

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 43b: ‘He may not go out wearing patched shoes. This supports the statement of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, as Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said: It is disgraceful for a Torah scholar to go out wearing patched shoes. The Gemara challenges: Is that so? Didn’t Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba himself go out wearing patched shoes? Mar Zutra, son of Rav Naḥman, said: It is only prohibited when the shoe has a patch upon a patch. And we only said this with regard to patches on the upper part of the shoe but if the patch is on the sole, this does not apply. And with regard to patches on the upper part of the shoe, we only said this when he is out on the road, but in his house, we need not be concerned. And we only said this…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:113, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 43b) to illuminate his teaching here (“Or: taking giant strides is forbidden Berakhot 43b save for a mitzvah; and Jacob went to marry and fulfill procreation; yet Jacob’s matriarchal lineage had an established presumption of barrenness requiring miracles;...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And it is known that the initial entrance of everything is from Chokhmah, which is the perceivable emergence termed "existence from nothingness," called Abba. However, Keter is the concealed root and acts as an encompassing light (makif), and in evil this reflects all extraneous thoughts that enter and flit spontaneously into the brain, causing confusion.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And the Lord said in His heart: I will not again...” To understand the expression “in His heart”—as stated in the Zohar (Lech Lecha 83a): in the heart resides the spark of vitality (kusta de-chiyuta), the heart being the life-point of the whole body; and so the great tzaddikim of the generation are the heart of their generation, serving as the spark of life for all, as in Berakhot (6b): “The whole world was created only to accompany this one; even for the sake of a single tzaddik the world was created.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yevamot 64b: ‘Rava said to him: No, there are unattributed mishnayot in accordance with each opinion, and he resolved for you that the halakha is in accordance with each opinion in particular cases. With regard to marriage and lashings the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that two occurrences are sufficient for a presumption. Concerning set patterns of menstrual bleeding and a forewarned ox, the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel that a presumption is established after three occurrences.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:113, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yevamot 64b) to illuminate his teaching here (“yet Jacob’s matriarchal lineage had an established presumption of barrenness requiring miracles; once assured by God “and your seed shall be as the dust of the earth” ibid. 28:14, he ran with joyous strides:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And in the case of Hannah in particular, this was the reason she was initially barren and her rival provoked her, until she shook worlds with her prayer and dedicated him by vow to the Blessed Name, until through this she merited to give birth to this soul which was already prepared to emerge, needing only this human awakening from below.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. And the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep...” In the Holy Zohar (Bo 39b), Rabbi Yitzchak said: The Torah should not have begun except from “This month shall be unto you the beginning of months” (Exodus 12:2) — what is the reason? Because it is the renewal / beginning of the moon, etc.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 28:14: ‘Your descendants shall be as the dust of the earth; you shall spread out to the west and to the east, to the north and to the south. All the families of the earth shall bless themselves by you and your descendants.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:113, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 28:14) to illuminate his teaching here (“yet Jacob’s matriarchal lineage had an established presumption of barrenness requiring miracles; once assured by God “and your seed shall be as the dust of the earth” ibid. 28:14, he ran with joyous strides:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For all these holinesses achieved by man as a mortal are bounded within the finite limits of human life in this world; for even though supernal holiness from Hashem is boundless, an inheritance without borders; nevertheless, being received according to the capacity of the vessel, man can receive only within finite boundaries. And the mystery of Jacob's heritage: "and you shall spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south" (Bereishis 28:14)—means breaking through every boundary and fence.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And then he was promised (ibid., vv. 11–15): “Moreover the Lord tells you that the Lord will make you a house: when your days are fulfilled, and you shall sleep with your fathers, I will set up your seed after you, who shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for My name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever... but My mercy shall not depart from him.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 29:2: ‘There before his eyes was a well in the open. Three flocks of sheep were lying there beside it, for the flocks were watered from that well. The stone on the mouth of the well was large.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:114, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 29:2) to illuminate his teaching here (““And behold three flocks of sheep lying there by it” Genesis 29:2: Jacob considered that a single shepherd might halt by chance to sell sheep, but three flocks established an enduring practice, ruling out mere...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And Jacob our father, peace be upon him, is the middle line, grasping both sides—at times this way and at times that way; and therefore he said: "the God Who shepherds me, etc.," in that he follows like sheep behind the shepherd, and therefore he merited greater fruitful multiplication and begot immediately. Nonetheless, he is likewise called a Father to the nation and is among the unyielding 'foundations of the earth,' and therefore Rachel was barren, yet she was the beloved.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And the meaning is: a person might question — since all of creation descended from His divine Word, which is eternally living, enduring, boundless, and infinite, surely His manifested Word should likewise appear eternally living, enduring, and boundless; yet in this physical world it sometimes appears as though severed from His divine Word, and this suggests that the King of kings does not will His holy Name to be associated with degradation.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 9:8: ‘Do not rebuke scoffers, for they will hate you;Reprove the wise, and they will love you.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:114, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 9:8) to illuminate his teaching here (“and he asked whether they had peaceful relations with Laban, seeking to rebuke their idleness, yet hesitant lest they be scoffers: “Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate you” Proverbs 9:8. Jacob assumed that since...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Unlike a harlot, who is brazen-faced, and speaks; as it says, “you had a harlot’s forehead, you refused to be ashamed” (Yirmeyah 3:3), you refused to be ashamed.” From Yirmeyahu’s rebuke of Israel’s faithlessness (ch. 3), likening her to a wanton wife. Rashi: the “harlot’s forehead” is brazenness — the unblushing face of one who refuses to be shamed. R’ Tzadok’s use: the harlot is az panim (brazen-faced), the very opposite of the eishes chayil, whose middah is modesty and bushah; Knesses Yisrael’s true splendor is her shame, the concealed Hod., and “the woman of folly is boisterous” (Mishlei 9:13) [homiyah]; she is naive [simplicity itself] and knows nothing.”
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 3:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: "And Hashem said to Avram: Go for yourself, etc., to the land that I will show you," (Genesis 12:1), "If you are wise, you are wise for yourself; and if you scoff, you alone shall bear it" (Proverbs 9:12). It is stated upon this in the holy Zohar (Vayeitzei 163a): When a man becomes wise in Torah, the benefit is his own, for to the Torah he cannot add even a single letter; 'and if you scoff, you alone shall bear it'—for from the praise of the Torah nothing is diminished, etc.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Batra 110a: ‘Rather, this is how the matter should be resolved: If his mother’s father came from the family of Joseph, his mother’s mother came from the family of Yitro, and if his mother’s father came from the family of Yitro, his mother’s mother came from the family of Joseph, so while his mother was descended from Joseph on one side and from Yitro on the other, Pinehas was a more distant relative to Yitro than Jonathan was. Based on this conclusion, the language of the verse is also precise, as it is written: “And Elazar, Aaron’s son, took one of the daughters of Putiel” (Exodus 6:25). Conclude from the wording of the verse that Pinehas was descended from two men who were referred to as Puti:…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:114, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 110a) to illuminate his teaching here (“Jacob assumed that since Laban was his mother’s brother, and sons usually resemble the mother’s brothers Bava Batra 110a, Laban must be righteous, wherefore Scripture repeatedly calls him “his mother's brother.” The...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Sefer HaZikhronot, Mitzvot, Positive Commandment 2, Chapter 1 5 (§4)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: However, regarding his own son — it appears that the mourner should circumcise even if another is available, for performing a mitzvah personally is greater than through an agent; yet an onen should not circumcise even his own son where another is present, as he is exempt from all commandments. And a claim of familial closeness is no valid claim to bestow it upon him; rather, he should give it to whoever is more righteous and a greater scholar (and also "better is a near neighbor than a distant brother").
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 12:9
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And the phenomenon that sometimes a righteous man fathers a wicked son, stems from evil lingering in his heart's depth that has not yet been refined. And that is: because all creatures were created with an innate lack; yet man on his part must ensure that at least the deficiency does not expand more than it existed upon his emergence from his mother's womb, rather conceal it lest it show outward, as written (Exodus 28:42): “And you shall make them linen breeches to cover their nakedness.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Taanit 23b: ‘The two Sages had one final set of queries for Abba Ḥilkiyya. And what is the reason that the clouds began to form on that side where the Master’s wife stood before your own side? He explained: Because my wife is frequently at home, and she gives bread to the poor, and therefore her provision of benefit to the needy is immediate, i.e., soon after the rains fall she is able to provide the needy with provisions. Accordingly, her prayers are answered without delay. In contrast, I give money to the poor, and consequently, the benefit of my gift is not immediate, i.e., it takes a lot of time before the rainfall results in my ability to give money to the poor. Alternatively, her prayers may…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:114, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Taanit 23b) to illuminate his teaching here (“The Sages noted Ta'anit 23b: if a scholar is hated by his townsmen it is because he rebukes them, which applies to scoffers; whereas the wise love their rebuker: “rebuke a wise man, and he will love you” Proverbs...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: In contrast, Yom Tov which 'Israel sanctifies' operates through active effort; and the rationale for the cessation of labor there is because on Yom Tov a renewed sanctity is added through Israel sanctifying it, and that added sanctity takes root in the pristine sanctity of Shabbat— namely the sanctity of Hashem Who is the Root of all from which all existence suckles— and through that addition of holiness it likewise becomes a fixed and permanent sanctity.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As in the shattered worlds hinted in the Kings of Edom (Genesis 36:31), where concerning all of them it is written “and he reigned... and he died,” save for the final king; Zohar Naso (142a) noting: because concerning him it is written: “and his wife's name...”—here female cleaved to male and sweetened one another, which is not written of the others — marking the inception of the World of Rectification in human form, the vessel strengthened relative to the light; hence “and he died” is omitted, this being enduring existence.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 9:8: ‘Do not rebuke scoffers, for they will hate you;Reprove the wise, and they will love you.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:114, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 9:8) to illuminate his teaching here (“The Sages noted Ta'anit 23b: if a scholar is hated by his townsmen it is because he rebukes them, which applies to scoffers; whereas the wise love their rebuker: “rebuke a wise man, and he will love you” Proverbs...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the owners stand beneath the priest, receiving holiness from him; so too one who brings a gift to a Torah scholar causes the scholar to attain Ruach HaKodesh, through whom bounty is channeled back to the giver. And this is realized solely through Torah, which is termed eating and drinking: "Come, eat of my bread, and drink of the wine which I have mingled" (Proverbs 9:5).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Regarding beasts it states “green herb”—the outer husk alone—for the animal has no portion in the hidden depths of the object, as it is written (Psalms 104:14): “He causes grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man, that he may bring forth bread out of the earth”; and “bread” is Torah, as it is written (Proverbs 9:5): “Come, eat of my bread,” which serves as a garment for the utterance of Anochi.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 29:6: ‘He continued, “Is he well?” They answered, “Yes, he is; and there is his daughter Rachel, coming with the flock.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:114, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 29:6) to illuminate his teaching here (“Hence Jacob asked: “Is it peace between you and him?”, and they answered: “It is peace”; whereupon he rebuked them: even if the flocks are your own, “it is not time that the cattle should be gathered together,” and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: In contrast, Rachel was "beautiful of form and fair to look upon," where all said: the younger daughter is for the younger son, for in the Revealed World (alma de-itgalya) she possessed manifest beauty of deeds. Nevertheless, the primary offspring issued from Leah, for the essence of true spiritual generation—innovating words of Torah and birthing holy souls for the will of Hashem—is entirely through the spiritual rung of repentance.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And as my revered grandfather remarked: Why is it that in the psalm (Psalms 148) “Praise Hashem from the heavens,” the waters under the heaven are not mentioned — it explicitly mentions the upper waters, so why not the lower waters as well? And even though it says there “deeps” (tehomot), “deeps” does not refer to the water itself, but to the deep oceanic vessel that holds the water. Why then does it not list the lower waters themselves?

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 29:7: “And he [Jacob] said: ‘Behold, it is yet high day, neither is it time that the cattle should be gathered together; water the sheep, and go and feed them.’” Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:114, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 29:7) to illuminate his teaching here (“whereupon he rebuked them: even if the flocks are your own, “it is not time that the cattle should be gathered together,” and withholding sheep from pasture inflicts cruelty to animals:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For prior to sin, as in the World to Come and with Jacob our father—in whom rectification was complete, over whom evil had no dominion and who therefore did not die—the very concept of "hating licentiousness" does not apply, because licentiousness does not exist at all. And this is the level of King David, concerning whom his adversaries slandered that he took a married woman, just as Jeroboam rebuked Solomon.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And God said: Let the waters under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear; and it was so.” It is stated in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 4:6): Why was “that it was good” not said on the second day? Because the work of the waters was not completed; therefore on the third day, when the work of the waters was finished, “that it was good” was doubled — once for the work of the waters and once for the work of the day.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 28:20: ‘Jacob then made a vow, saying, “If God remains with me, protecting me on this journey that I am making, and giving me bread to eat and clothing to wear,’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:115, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 28:20) to illuminate his teaching here (““And will give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on” Genesis 28:20: Jacob added this supplication beyond what Hashem had explicitly promised him; for there is a halakhic dispute in Bava Batra 9a: one opinion holds...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And our father Jacob, peace be upon him, asked solely: "and will give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on" (Bereishis 28:20); and the Sages stated concerning him likewise in Chullin (91a): "that the righteous cherish their money more than their bodies"; but not out of greed for money at all, but out of the need to provide sustenance for his children, that he not trouble his soul with financial worries; his petition being strictly within measured boundaries.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Then I will feed you the heritage of Jacob your father, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken”—the heritage of Jacob is an inheritance without boundaries, unbounded and limitless in its expansion. And the proof of this is “for the mouth of the Lord has spoken,” in that the Blessed Name explicitly warned against walking beyond the boundary to acquire anything; from which it is proven that the Commander Himself is endless and boundless, and His glory fills the entire universe.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Batra 9a: ‘If you wish, say that this distinction is derived via logical reasoning: This one who is hungry suffers, whereas that one who is in tattered clothing does not suffer in the same way. And if you wish, say instead that this distinction is derived from a verse. Here, it is written: “Is it not to share [paros] your bread with the hungry?” meaning, share it immediately, just as the word is read. Since the word is read with a samekh, Rav Yehuda does not understand it as alluding to examining the recipient. And there, it is written: “When you see the naked, that you cover him,” meaning, when it will be clearly apparent to you, after you have investigated the matter and found that the supplicant…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:115, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Batra 9a) to illuminate his teaching here (“for there is a halakhic dispute in Bava Batra 9a: one opinion holds that we investigate the legitimacy of applicants for clothing but not for food; while the opposing opinion holds the reverse; and Jacob humbly...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Even though our Sages stated in Bava Batra 9a: "if one does not merit, his resources go to the oppressive rulers (merudim)," that is because when one merits, he has no need for this; however, if he did not merit, there is great atonement through the oppressive rulers, as is known from the Zohar that the scapegoat sent away is the mystical secret of the gift that Jacob sent to Esau.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: The allusion in specifying “a drop like a mustard seed” is because mustard is known to harm honey (Mishnah Bava Batra 25a); and honey symbolizes the Name Ehyeh, which bees gather from blossoms before the fruit has formed; as in Sotah (48b), where Rav Sheshet translates: “as bees fly across the heights of the world and gather honey from mountain herbs” — meaning honey is collected from uncultivated wild plants not yet edible human food, alluding to the unactualized Will wherein the root of sweetness abides.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 28:14: ‘Your descendants shall be as the dust of the earth; you shall spread out to the west and to the east, to the north and to the south. All the families of the earth shall bless themselves by you and your descendants.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 1:115, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 28:14) to illuminate his teaching here (“and Jacob humbly doubted whether he was fully righteous; the promise of numerous descendants being no proof of personal perfection since even the wicked multiply; and protection from peril being general providence;...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And therefore Jacob merited and inherited the world without bound or limitation, and it is written of him (Genesis 28:14): 'And you shall spread abroad to the west, and to the east, etc.,' meaning that he is empowered to burst forth his holiness into every place, even beyond the geographic borders of the Land, such that wherever Israel may be dispersed, the Holy Shechinah abides in their midst.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “For the rod of the wicked shall not rest upon the lot of the righteous”—the temporarily triumphant wicked possessing no permanent dominion over him, being shielded from accusation. And this was the case with Noah, who was a tzaddik not yet fully refined in his heart's root, yet because he embraced constriction, restraining himself from evil, Hashem sheltered him until the wrath passed; because Noah did not wish to reveal and clarify the hidden depths of his heart, and an accusation can arise only over what has been revealed in action.

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For in this world man yearns for light and it is precious (rare), because “precious” designates that which man cannot produce on his own, which is spiritual light; for it is not within man's power to illuminate his own darkness wherein he is submerged, this being solely in the hand of Hashem, since “a prisoner cannot free himself from prison” (Berakhot 5b).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 3:24: ‘humankind was driven out; and east of the garden of Eden were stationed the cherubim and the fiery ever-turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:5, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 3:24) to illuminate his teaching here (“to "guard the way to the Tree of Life"— this refers to Torah. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the Cherubim and the flaming sword were placed "to keep the way of the Tree of Life" (Bereishis 3:24), for even after all the repentance, the 130 years of fasts, and the abstention from his wife and desires, he could not rectify enough to return to Gan Eden and eat from the Tree of Life to merit eternal life; because this defilement (zuhama), once absorbed into the physical body, has no remedy except burial, that he return to the dust as he was.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “The tree of life also in the midst of the garden.” And it is necessary to understand: Was not the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil also in the midst of the garden, as it is written: “And of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the garden, God said: You shall not eat of it”?! The explanation is: from the perspective of the Name Havayah, the Tree of Life was in the midst of the garden; whereas regarding the Tree of Knowledge the Name Elohim is written.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And for those who turn left within the Torah, it becomes a potion of death (Shabbat 88b); but for those who turn right within her: "wine gladdens the heart of man" (Tehillim 104:15), and wine makes one wise, this virtue belonging exclusively unto the seed of Israel!
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 11:10
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Because his heart was steadfastly trusting in Hashem that there exists with Hashem a sanctity grand and broader than the sea, greater than the measure of human intellect's grasp, life of lives unto infinity without end, such that it is beyond his power even to anticipate and hope for such holiness; and the Holy One revealed Himself to him and said: "I am the master of the palace"— meaning: to you and to future generations walking in your footsteps I will show that I govern all matters in the world.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Micah 7:20: ‘You will keep faith with Jacob,Loyalty to Abraham,As You promised on oath to our fathersIn days gone by.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:5, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Micah 7:20) to illuminate his teaching here (“and along the middle axis stands 'truth to Jacob', which is the Torah of which 'truth' is written, lest one who turns leftward also stretch out his hand and eat from the Tree of Life and live forever; rather, one...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Never permitting the essential core of Judaism to be assimilated among the gentiles or allowing blemish to touch the ultimate soul-root. Therefore there exists within every descendant of Israel the capacity to be awakened through the memory of the day of death and the knowledge that another world exists, returning unto the Blessed Name in truth through this, since he possesses an indelible point belonging to that eternal world; and that inner point is drawn from the letter Yud of the Name Havayah, blessed be He.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Yet “the lips of the wise shall preserve them”—meaning that the wise reserve this profound metaphysical realization strictly within their silent contemplation, as it is written (Micah 7:5): “Do not trust in a friend, put no confidence in a guide”; for the wise never rely in practice upon this radical truth, knowing that the Blessed Name concealed His light, and from man’s vantage point unchecked indulgence is classified as sin; since relying upon absolute divine determinism is valid only retroactively in thought—such as a penitent reflecting on the past who must never despair of return—whereas regarding the future, one must never rely upon such assumptions.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Isaiah 45:19: ‘I did not speak in secret,At a site in a land of darkness;I did not say to the stock of Jacob,“Seek Me out in a wasteland”—I GOD, who foretell reliably,Who announce what is true.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:6, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Isaiah 45:19) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Isaiah 45:19: "I said not to the seed of Jacob who cling to the middle axis, 'Seek Me in chaos'": chaos refers to the green line the hue of tekhelet, signifying awe which encircles the entire universe.”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Through Israel's proliferation holiness expanding in every generation. And so I received: that although outer generations decline, the inner point of the heart becomes increasingly refined and luminous in each generation until the final redemption; for holiness bears fruit and fruit of fruit, continually increasing, this being the holy increase of Israel, for which the world was created: "He created it not a waste" [Isaiah 45:18], never saying to Jacob's seed "Seek Me in vain" [ibid. 45:19].
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As in the Zohar (Vayelech 284a): “Zmirot is as you say: ‘lo tizmor’”; and as it is written (Isaiah 45:19): “I said not unto the seed of Jacob: Seek Me in vain (tohu).” For once Hashem chose Jacob and cut His covenant with him, He desires the enduring preservation of Israel, not their total dissolution. Even the commandment of sanctifying the Name (Kiddush Hashem)—where one must surrender life for His holiness—applies only in public before ten Jews, where an enduring legacy remains as God’s Name is magnified publicly, etching holiness in the hearts of onlookers.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Makkot 24a: ‘Isaiah then established the 613 mitzvot upon two, as it is stated: “So says the Lord: Observe justice and perform righteousness” (Isaiah 56:1). Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: The greatness of this matter — is beyond measure; and there is no need to elaborate, for "knowledge is easy to the discerning," as this is the root of the entire Torah and all the commandments; for if there is no God, Heaven forbid — where is there a place for Torah and commandments? And our Rabbis of blessed memory said, at the end of Makkot (folio 24a): "Amos came and established them upon one, as it is stated: 'Seek Me and live'; it was objected," etc., "rather: Habakkuk came and established them upon one, as it is stated: 'And the righteous person shall live by his faith.'"
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Writings, Proverbs 8:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “By me kings reign, and princes decree justice” (Proverbs 8:15): the sovereignty of the Torah precedes and governs all earthly orders. When a person cleaves to the primordial wisdom of the Torah, he attains true sovereignty over the inclinations of his heart and discerns the straight path in every circumstance.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 1:1: ‘Rabbi Hoshaya the Great began: “I was with Him as an amon, a delight day after day…” (Proverbs 8:30) – amon means a child’s caretaker, amon means covered, amon means hidden, and some say amon means greatness. Amon means a child’s caretaker, as it says: “As a caretaker [omen] carries a nursing child” (Numbers 11:12). Amon means covered, as it says: “Those covered [ha’emunim] in scarlet…” (Lamentations 4:5). Amon means hidden, as it says: “He was omen Hadassa” (Esther 2:7). 'Amon' means hidden away in...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And from this flow differences in apprehending the powers of creation, great variations existing in perceiving sight, taste, touch, and the like: though agreeing on generalities, they diverge in particulars. Just as with the Torah, the blueprint of the cosmos (Bereishit Rabbah 1:1): while its general principles are undisputed, detailed halakhot diverge according to the differing perspectives of the disputants; so it is with the universe fashioned after its mold, as is clear to the discerning.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And likewise it is stated in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 1:5): Anyone who comes and says, “This royal palace was built on a site of sewers, dung heaps, and foul garbage” — does he not slander and degrade it? So too, anyone who comes and says, “This world was created out of primordial chaos (tohu and va-bohu)” — does he not degrade it?! Astonishing!

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 11:2: ‘When arrogance appears, disgrace follows,But wisdom is with those who are unassuming.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:6, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 11:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Proverbs 11:2: "and with the modest is wisdom", for Moses within is Jacob without, for this world is termed the World of Falsehood and the truth is hidden away;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Whoever brings merit to the guilty is likewise empowered to rectify this sin, for he is titled "he that wins souls" (Proverbs 11:30), as our Sages expounded on the verse "and the souls that they had gotten in Haran" (Genesis 12:5), that it is as though he created them, and soul restores soul and regarding the sin of wasted seed, when willful sins are converted into merits and those souls are redeemed into holiness, vast divine influx is added, and it turns out that he brought merit to the guilty through this, his sin mirroring the very pattern of his rectification.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:21–22
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As it is written (Proverbs 11:10): "and when the wicked perish, there is joy", and as brought on this in the holy Zohar (Noach 61a). Different was Avraham our Father, peace be upon him, who was cleaving at the root continually unto Hashem, blessed be He, and the depth of his heart was filled with the will of Hashem without any deviation on his part, and he was swift and fervent to fulfill His will, blessed be He, and as it is written of him (Genesis 22:3): "And Avraham rose early in the morning, etc.,"

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: II Chronicles 17:6: ‘His mind was elevated in GOD’s ways. And certainly, one who is in absolute, passive lowliness, how could he say this? and he would remain content with the meager deeds and Torah in his possession. And regarding this it is said of Jehoshaphat: 'And his heart was lifted up in the ways of Hashem' (II Chronicles 17:6), and this is stated uniquely concerning him, because regarding him our Sages expounded (Ketubot 103b): ''He honors those who fear Hashem'—.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 20:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And I will bless them that bless you, and him that curses you will I curse” (Genesis 12:3). The concept is: behold then, in the days of Avraham our Father, when he began innovating the path of Hashem in the world, the multitude split into two factions: friends and foes. Some loved him with all their heart, and he found favor in their eyes for inaugurating a new path for their enduring good, which they had never known, having walked until then in ways of darkness and slippery slope.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Kiddushin 32b: ‘The Gemara asks: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili? Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: As they taught (Kiddushin 32b): 'His awe must be upon you,' and a king who waives his honor, etc.; without this there is no concept of kingship. This is the creation of the sixth day: man, who rises above all other earthly creatures (Chagigah 13b). This is the goal of every form of praise—that there be created beings who recognize the Creator.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For one the king decreed that he be sustained from the royal palace, and for the other he decreed, “If he does not toil, he shall not eat.” That second servant sat bewildered and despondent, etc. For in truth, from the perspective of Hashem, there is no difference between the upper waters and the lower waters, because at their root they are unified as one.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 1: ‘Rabbi Yona said in the name of Rabbi Levi: Why was the world created with the letter beit? – in the beginning.” It is because just as the beit is closed on all [three of] its sides but open in its front, so, you do not have permission to ask: What is below, what is above, what was before, and what is after,2:1. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For all His modes of governance emerged with creation, since before the world was created He and His Name were One in absolute simplicity; only that the manifestation of varied attributes and diverse ways of governance emerged at creation, when His simple will decreed diverse creatures; and the Torah is the blueprint of Creation, as taught in Bereishit Rabbah (1:1).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: This means that in the narrative of Genesis, God's glory lies in apportioning vitality to each creature, concerning which it is said “to conceal a thing,” for as the Talmud states: “The King does not desire His Name to be mentioned upon a dunghill.” Meaning, were man to pry philosophically into this, he would wonder: why was imperfection embedded in nature, forcing him to refine himself through arduous toil, rather than being created in full perfection?

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Pirkei Avot 1:2: ‘Shimon the Righteous was one of the last of the men of the great assembly. He used to say: the world stands upon three things: the Torah, the Temple service, and the practice of acts of piety.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:7, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Pirkei Avot 1:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is the meaning of Avot 1:2: "On three things the world stands": upon the Torah—which is the very existence of life; and upon divine service—which is the channel through which life is apportioned and reaches...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Such is their descending order in Pirkei Avot (1:2): "Upon three things the world stands: upon the Torah"—wisdom in the brain; "upon the Service"—in the heart [which was also the physical sacrificial service of Priests and Levites in the Temple]; "and upon Acts of Lovingkindness"—in practical action, as noted above. Except that the Mishnah there reversed the order of spiritual ascent, listing them downward from above to below.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And Noah begot three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.” In the Holy Zohar (Noach 62a): A parable of a man, etc.: this one is righteous, this one is wicked, and this one is intermediate. My revered father, my master and teacher, of blessed memory, explained regarding this that the primary beginning of the World of Rectification (Olam HaTikkun) began from Noah onward.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yoma 38b: ‘Apropos the righteous, Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: No righteous person departs from this world until another comparable righteous person is created, as it is stated: “And the sun rises and the sun sets” (Ecclesiastes 1:5); before the sun sets the new sun has already risen. Before the sun of Eli was extinguished, the sun of Samuel of Ramah had already shone (see I Samuel, chapter 3), and so on throughout the generations. And Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: The Holy One, Blessed be He, saw that righteous people were few, so He arose and planted some of them in each and every generation to ensure the presence of at least one righteous person in each…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:7, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yoma 38b) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Yoma 38b: "And the righteous is the foundation of the world". For if not a single one is found, the world reverts to chaos and void, as occurred with Sodom and the Generation of the Flood,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this utterance stands enduringly within all souls of all generations, who were all present at the assembly at Mount Sinai. And in every single generation, as they emerge into physical actuality in this world, this utterance likewise emerges into actuality within their heart at the moment they initially turn toward the words of Torah and spiritual exertion.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And likewise the wicked sustained by that attribute expand with turbulent deluge. As in the generation of Ahab, governed through Elijah's attribute of zealousness (“I have been very jealous”), opposite which Ahab expanded in idolatrous frenzy. And concerning this it is said: “When the whirlwind passes”—when Hashem sheds that specific garment, “the wicked is no more,” perishing as Hashem engages another attribute; “but the righteous is an everlasting foundation”—the tzaddik being the surviving residue (reshimu) elevated from that entire garment.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bereshit Rabbah 14: ‘It [man’s soul] is called by five names: nefesh (Genesis 2:7), ruaḥ (Ezekiel 37:14), neshama (Genesis 2:7), yeḥida (Psalms 22:21), ḥaya (Psalms 143:3). Nefesh – this refers to blood, as it is stated: “For blood is the soul [nefesh]” (Deuteronomy 12:23). Ruaḥ – because it ascends and descends, as it is stated: “Who knows the spirit of the sons of man? Does it ascend upward?” (Ecclesiastes 3:21). also means wind, which ascends and descends. Neshama – this refers to man’s intellect, as people say: Intellect is good. Ḥaya – because all of one’s limbs may die, but it [the soul] remains alive [ḥaya] in the body. Yeḥida – because all of one’s limbs are in pairs, but it [the soul] is solitary…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:8, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Bereshit Rabbah 14) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this corresponds to the five soul-levels Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah, Yechidah mentioned in Bereishit Rabbah 14: for as is known, Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah correspond to thought, speech, and action seated...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And these five worlds correspond to the five rungs and titles of the soul enumerated in Bereishit Rabbah (14:9): Nefesh—the physical blood; Ruach—which ascends and descends within; Neshamah—the breath/intellect (da'at); Chayah—which remains living when the limbs die; and Yechidah—the singular transcendent essence; see there at length.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 31:9
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And the concept of Avraham our Father descending into Egypt is akin to what is brought in the Midrash (Shocher Tov, Psalms 62): This soul, at every hour that it ascends and descends seeking to depart from man, how does it remain inside him?! Rather the Holy One, “the whole earth is full of His glory”, places it within his body; and when it comes to depart, it beholds its Creator and withdraws back.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Batra 14a: ‘The baraita continues: And as for the tablets, their length was six handbreadths, their width was six handbreadths, and their thickness was three handbreadths. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is the exacting of payment for sins that is collected from the righteous in this world; for concerning literal worldly afflictions other rules apply, as our Sages stated (Moed Katan 28a): children, life, and sustenance depend not on merit but on heavenly constellation. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Like all miracles wherein the Blessed Name alters nature for the righteous, so is the absolute nullification of the yetzer hara from the heart; as David HaMelech declared: "and my heart is slain within me" (Tehillim 109:22), having slain the yetzer hara through fasting (Bava Batra 17a); this foreshadowing the Future when the sin of Adam HaRishon will be fully rectified; and all orders of nature that were distorted on the sixth day following Adam's sin will be restored to their pristine state before the Fall.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 31:7 (§2)

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 104a: ‘The Gemara cites another midrash that also deals with the letters of the alphabet. Gimmel reish: He defiled his body [gufo]; shall I have mercy [araḥem] on him? The word comprised of the letters gimmel and reish in Aramaic means licentiousness. To this point, the Gemara interpreted the…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:11, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 104a) to illuminate his teaching here (“as it is written Shabbat 104a: "It is the way of the benevolent to run after the impoverished", and he is not restricted by the standard fence termed the strict letter of the law. And this explains the matter of...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Therefore the Name Havayah represents Lovingkindness (Chesed)—infinite expansion without end, as stated in Shabbat (104a): "The way of the benevolent is to pursue the poor." That is: since the whole earth is full of His glory and there is none beside Him, all human actions are animated by His power veiled within them; and were Havayah revealed openly in this world, there would be no room to judge man for his deeds (for human agency would dissolve); and this is not the place to elaborate.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this is what is stated in Midrash Tanchuma (Bereishit 1): “‘His locks are curled (taltalim)’ (Song of Songs 5:11)—upon every single stroke and serif of the letters are mounds upon mounds (tilei tilim) of halakhot.” Meaning, within the word “Bereishit” it is hinted that you must never deviate from the divine command, fulfilling “in whose spirit there is no guile,” ensuring one never alters a Dalet to a Reish or a Beit to a Chaf (as will be explained below in section 2).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 6:9: ‘This is the line of Noah.—Noah was a righteous man; he was blameless in his age; Noah walked with God.—’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:11, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 6:9) to illuminate his teaching here (“whereas Noah was "a righteous man tzaddik, etc." Genesis 6:9, and this is the deeper significance of the Ark, which served as an enclosure so that he would not gaze upon evil, and as written in the Zohar Noach 63a”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is designated as illuminating before Him, blessed be He, by publicizing His divine light; and not like Noah: "with God walked Noah" (Genesis 6:9), meaning strictly what he received from Methuselah and what he taught him and instructed him to perform; he was simply not like the Generation of the Flood who willfully transgressed, while he did not transgress.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And so it is stated in the Holy Zohar (Shelach 169a): In the future, the ultimate resurrection of the dead will be generated from the spiritual residue of the bones (hevlei de-garmei) and from the deep inner grief/yearning (itzavon) of man. That is to say, for in truth it is written (Genesis 6:6): “And He was grieved at His heart.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Zohar, Noach 12:76-13:85: ‘But, you may object further, the ark was exposed to full view in the midst of the world through which the destroyer was roaming. How, then, could it accept upon itself to harm Israel through it, and all the more so to destroy them from the world entirely, Heaven forbid? Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” In the Holy Zohar (Bo 39b): Rabbi Yitzchak said: The Torah needed to be written only from “This month shall be unto you” (Exodus 12:2), what is the reason? Because it marks the renewal of the moon, and therefore the Torah should have been written from there, for behold, with the Holy One, blessed be He, the matter is bound.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Pirkei Avot 4:2: ‘Ben Azzai said: Be quick in performing a minor commandment as in the case of a major one, and flee from transgression; For one commandment leads to another commandment, and transgression leads to another transgression; For the reward for performing a commandment is another commandment and the reward for committing a transgression is a transgression.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:11, Rav Tzadok draws upon this midrashic exposition (Pirkei Avot 4:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“as is known Avot 4:2: "The recompense of a sin is a sin", for the retribution and the sin are essentially one, which is why they taught Sotah 8b that all punishments operate measure for measure, because they are...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: But "one transgression drags another in its wake" (Avos 4:2), and he sought to hide and flee from the Blessed Name; when he saw himself in darkness unable to see, he deluded himself that he was likewise unseen, imagining he could deceive supernal Knowledge; compounding his fault, not internalizing: "Can any hide himself in secret places that I shall not see him? says Hashem" (Yirmiyah 23:24); for Hashem knows what is in the darkness (Daniel 2:22) and in the lowest depths; and also: "if I make my bed in the nether-world, behold, You are there" (Tehillim 139:8), and "whither shall I flee from Your presence?" (ibid. 139:7).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Therefore from Hashem's perspective even a good intention of man is never lost, and an enduring remnant is preserved for human labor achieved within mortal grasp. Yet from man's perspective, true ownership and enduring reward depend upon the joy he experiences in knowing that it is truly the toil of his own hands; as written (Exodus 31:13): “that you may know that I am the Lord that sanctifies you”; and as taught in Avot (3:14): “Beloved is man that he was created in the image of God; an especially great love was made known to him in that he was created in the image” —.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sotah 8b: ‘The mishna teaches: If she was wearing gold adornments or other jewelry, they are removed from her. The Gemara asks: Isn’t this obvious? Therefore, the…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:11, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 8b) to illuminate his teaching here (“which is why they taught Sotah 8b that all punishments operate measure for measure, because they are literally the same entity: it is the dross of a supernal attribute— in this hue it manifests as an act of sin,”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: The Sages measured this required volume as forty se'ah, because a se'ah is the maximum biblical measure applied to sins and transgressions, as taught in Sotah (8b) on the verse: "B'sas'ah (in full measure)—I know only of a se'ah," etc.; for the domain of transgressions and sins is confined exclusively to this physical world, as recorded at the end of Sukkah (52a), that in the Time to Come the evil inclination will be slaughtered; and in Bereishit Rabbah (parashah 11): "He who does not observe the Sabbath here [in this world] will observe it there [in Gehenna]," etc..
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: That is, one who is foolish, when Hashem gives validation to his service, immediately assumes self-importance and boldness. However, one who is wise claims no personal power for himself, but hedges and disciplines himself all the more. And this is: “Tohu is something that confounds people” — meaning that creatures can be misled into drawing haughty self-assurance from it.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 6:16: ‘Make an opening for daylight in the ark, and terminate it within a cubit of the top. Put the entrance to the ark in its side; make it with bottom, second, and third decks.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 6:16) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is the meaning of Genesis 6:16: "Bottom, second, and third stories shall you make it": and its height was thirty cubits, for as is known, each story is comprised of ten. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the perfection of the Torah was realized in Jacob our father whose bed was undefiled, personifying the attribute of Truth, which is Torah [Berakhot 5b]. Nevertheless, since Torah issues from Gevurah, the root of its transmission commenced in Isaac. And because the core purpose of Torah is striving in mitzvot and good deeds, which are the primary offspring of the righteous (Tanchuma Noach; Rashi on Genesis 6:9), therefore it is likewise the primary impetus for striving after physical offspring.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “And Noah began to be a husbandman, and he planted a vineyard; and he drank of the wine, and was drunken.” My revered father, of blessed memory, explained: Noah expanded himself here into the three matters that were hinted in the architecture of the Ark, concerning which it was said to him (Genesis 6:16): “with lower, second, and third stories shall you make it,” which were explained above (section 19) as signifying the counsel given to him to enter into the three traits that the Holy One loves: one who does not become angry, one who does not become intoxicated, and one who forgives his grievances.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Job 11:9: ‘Its measure is longer than the earthAnd broader than the sea.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Job 11:9) to illuminate his teaching here (“And the length and breadth reflect what is written Job 11:9: "Longer than the earth is its measure, and broader than the sea": for from the element of Earth derive laziness, gloom, anger, and envy, as is known. Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And it is already established by early masters that the entire Torah is comprised of mystical Names of the Holy One, Blessed be He; and this is the Written Torah, concerning which it is said: "Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea" (Job 11:9), having no boundary in its transcendent concealment, which is the very essence of the Torah as it was originally inscribed as black fire upon white fire (Jerusalem Talmud, Shekalim 6:1) prior to enclothing itself in material terms.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: The meaning is as my revered father explained: if a man seeks to conceal his sin, forgetting what he distorted, Hashem reminds him, exposing his guilt in public judgment; as when Adam hid himself among the trees, and Hashem called unto him: “Where are you?” Conversely, if a person remembers his sin, fulfilling “and my sin is ever before me,” Hashem behaves as though forgetting, looking upon that sin no more; as written (Job 11:11): “He sees iniquity also, will He not then consider it?”.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 1:4: ‘God saw that the light was good, and God separated the light from the darkness.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 1:4) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is Genesis 1:4: "And God separated between the light and the darkness"— darkness being gloom, as it is written Isaiah 60:2: "darkness shall cover the earth", and Genesis 15:12 "behold, a dread, great darkness",”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the power of hearing is the reverse: “the one heard acts upon the hearer” — and the essential meaning of “hearing” is “receiving of matters,” and it is a “receiving power.” And therefore, in the Account of Creation, “seeing is mentioned immediately” — at the creation of the light it says, “and God saw” (Bereishis 1:4), ” — “and God saw the light, that it was good, and God separated between the light and the darkness.”
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And afterward it is written: “And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night”—this is created darkness emerging from the side of creation, meaning that the Blessed Name instituted a constricting attribute ensuring that the light would not expand beyond containment; and this is the attribute of Gevurah (Strength/Restraint), the trait of Isaac our Father, peace be upon him, which is termed “darkness”; for the earthly garment of the primordial darkness is spiritual constriction and reverent awe.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the primary head of this influx flows to the king of the nation, who is the head of the people and foremost among the recipients; just as the culmination of the emanator is likewise the attribute of Malchus as is known; and Nissan is the inception of the renewal of light following darkness and concealment, wherein "For, behold, darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the peoples; but upon you Hashem will shine, and His glory shall be seen upon you" (Yeshayah 60:2).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Noah was a righteous man.” In the Holy Zohar (Noach 59a): Rabbi Chiyya opened and said: “Your people also shall be all righteous”—whoever guards this covenant upon which the world endures is called righteous (tzaddik); from where do we derive this? From Joseph, because he guarded the covenant, etc., he merited to be called righteous; and therefore “Your people also shall be all righteous.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 15:12: ‘As the sun was about to set, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, and a great dark dread descended upon him.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 15:12) to illuminate his teaching here (“and Genesis 15:12 "behold, a dread, great darkness", and laziness as described regarding the darkness of Egypt; and light is its opposite and the rectification of darkness. In the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 44:21): Our father Avraham was sitting and wondering all that day, saying: “Which shall I choose: Gehenna or the subjugation of empires?” the Holy One said to Abraham: “Cut this coin (make a decisive choice)”, and gave him counsel to choose the subjugation of empires.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 5:2: ‘It is written (1Kings 17:1) “Elijah the Tisbite, from the inhabitants of Gilead, said to Aḥab: By the Living Eternal One, the God of Israel, before Whom I stood, there will not be dew nor rain these years except by my word.” Rebbi Berekhia said, Rebbi Yasa and the rabbis.
