And this is the boundary of length running from east to west, whence light and darkness emerge into the world...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For "if there is no discernment, from where is there separation?" (Havdalah), as our Sages of blessed memory taught (Yerushalmi Berakhot 5:2, 37a), and he cannot distinguish between good and evil, so how could he know how to repent?! And each person must undergo this sequence: "sees with his eyes" the eyes of his intellect, and afterward "and hears with his ears"— this is termed Chokhmah (Wisdom), that which one receives from others, and it is stated: "He gives wisdom unto the wise" (Daniel 2:21).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Yet within the human soul uniquely resides moral free will, unchained to any instinct without deliberate choice—the quintessential human form— whose union is not mere biological coupling, but face-to-face communion through moral counsel and choice. And the Generation of the Flood opposed the human archetype, as written: “for the earth was filled with violence,” translated by Onkelos: “robbers/snatchers” — lacking boundaries against encroaching upon a fellow's border.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 3:19: ‘By the sweat of your browShall you get bread to eat,Until you return to the ground—For from it you were taken.For dust, as in 2.7; cf. the second note there. you are,And to dust you shall return.”’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 3:19) to illuminate his teaching here (“mirroring what is written Genesis 3:19: "For dust you are", and therefore one must construct an even greater fence against it; and as our Sages taught Yevamot 102b: "'And He shall strengthen your bones'—this means...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the element of dust/earth was not counted there, because it represents the raw material substrate of every object, as stated (Genesis 3:19): "for dust you are, and unto dust shall you return," being the visible physical body and core matter of a thing. But these three elements are the concealed dimensions within every entity, and everything concealed constitutes an energetic, dynamic force and form (tzurah) to it, for matter is ever manifest while form is concealed; wherefore only these three are tallied.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Just as we find with Adam HaRishon, whom the Holy One asked after the sin (Genesis 3:11): “Have you eaten of the tree whereof I commanded you that you should not eat?” and he had no justification to answer: “Surely You created me and in Your power alone did I act!” because the concealment had already deepened so vastly within him that he felt his own autonomous choices caused him to sin against Hashem.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Yevamot 102b: ‘The Gemara challenges further: But with regard to that which is written: “And the Lord will guide you, and satisfy your soul in drought, and make your bones strong [yaḥalitz]” (Isaiah 58:11), and Rabbi Elazar said regarding that verse: This is the greatest of blessings, and Rava said it means: Strengthening of bones. This seems to indicate that the root of the word ḥalitza is referring to strengthening. The Gemara answers: Yes, it has this connotation, and it has this connotation, i.e., the root ḥ-l-tz sometimes connotes removal and sometimes connotes strengthening. But here, only one meaning is possible, as, if it enters your mind that ḥalitza here connotes strengthening, then let the…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Yevamot 102b) to illuminate his teaching here (“and as our Sages taught Yevamot 102b: "'And He shall strengthen your bones'—this means fortifying the limbs", and this is what is written in Proverbs 14:30: "and envy is rottenness of the bones"—the absence of...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And the root of the revelation of Keser Elyon, concealed from every creature in this world, is in the letter Yud alluding to the inception of existence ex nihilo from Ayin; and within the upper thorn of the Yud is hinted Ayin [Nothingness]; for the perception of Ayin is achieved through the Yesh [Being], which is Chochmah grasped within human intellect; and through the existence of Yesh mortals know that there exists a transcendent Ayin that creates that Yesh, wherefore Ayin is indicated in the thorn of the Yud.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 1:27
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this is why the house of Garmu were bound at the root, for 'bones' is translated into Aramaic as garmin, which connotes essence (atzmiyut), in that they were intimately close to the very essence of His will, blessed be He. And this is alluded to in their statement that they baked from within— which means they coronated Hashem over themselves from the depth of their heart's will; and they furthermore knew how to extract the bread from the oven— meaning that even after the bounty and finished product rested in their hand.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Proverbs 14:30: ‘A calm disposition gives bodily health;Passion is rot to the bones.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Proverbs 14:30) to illuminate his teaching here (“and this is what is written in Proverbs 14:30: "and envy is rottenness of the bones"—the absence of fortified limbs, this is the most exquisite of blessings. And 300 represents fencing for thought, speech, and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And so our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Sotah 5a): 'Basar' (flesh)—an acronym for Shame (bushah), Stench (seruchah), Maggots (rimmah); and these are the three chief negative traits encompassing all evils of the 365 prohibitions and their branches, namely: Envy, Lust, and Honor (Avot 4:21). Maggots (rimmah) alludes to envy, as written: "and envy is rottenness of the bones" (Proverbs 14:30), where the bone rots away and turns into maggots; and Stench (seruchah) alludes to bodily lust.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And in truth, the essence of man’s piercing the concealment is that he implants and establishes sanctity over all the operational limbs of his bodily actions; herein lies the focal point of man’s divine service. And this is the inner intent of the holy Ari, of blessed memory (Likutei Torah, Parashat Bereishit, s.v. Bereishit): “The Torah did not speak in the realm of Atzilut (Emanation), but only in Beriah (Creation).”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Psalms 12:7: ‘GOD’s words are pure words,silver purged in an earthen crucible,refined sevenfold.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Psalms 12:7) to illuminate his teaching here (“as written Psalms 12:7: "refined sevenfold"—meaning seven times seven, and I have explained elsewhere the inner reason; and likewise here: ten times ten is one hundred. And the element of Water generates desire, as...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: In the manner of the verse (Psalms 12:7): "purified seven times," for purification being sevenfold, ultimate purification is seven times seven (49). And so it is their custom to employ one hundred to signify the most consummate perfection, as in Shabbat (25b): "Who is wealthy? He who possesses 100 vineyards, 100 fields, and 100 servants" [and so they use one hundred as a grand archetype across the Talmud (Pesachim 89b; Chagigah 9b; Sotah 42b; Bava Kamma 27b), based on this rationale].
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Deuteronomy, Re'eh 9
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Count for yourself seven weeks, from the time the sickle is first put to the standing corn shall you begin to count seven weeks.” (Devarim, 16:9)“From the time the sickle is first put to the standing corn.” That is to say, at a time when man begins to march on towards victory he must possess a settled mind and make careful deliberations, for seven weeks represents great refinement.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Bava Kamma 17a: ‘The Gemara asks: But didn’t the Master say: Torah study is great because the study of Torah leads to one’s performance of the mitzvot? This indicates that the performance of mitzvot is considered of greater value than Torah study. If so, once Hezekiah had been praised with the fact that he fulfilled the mitzvot of the Torah, why mention that he studied it? The Gemara explains: This is not difficult: This statement of the Master is about studying the Torah for one’s own knowledge, and that unique praise given to King Hezekiah was about teaching the Torah to others.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Bava Kamma 17a) to illuminate his teaching here (“and therefore 'there is no water but Torah' Bava Kamma 17a, for the rectification of lust is through Torah, as I wrote elsewhere. And this is Genesis 1:7: "And He separated between the waters below the firmament and...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is by virtue of their inheriting the fixed faculties of all the nations among whom they were exiled. Therefore then: "He will make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert" (Isaiah 43:19), for the 'heart of stone' will be completely eradicated. In contrast, at the beginning, they immediately traveled a three days' journey and found no water, and our Sages of blessed memory expounded (Bava Kamma 17a): "water means Torah", because they were still characterized by the heart of stone.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Mei HaShiloach, Mei HaShiloach Anthology, Talmud, Berakhot 62b:1
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Concerning David’s restraint in the cave when Saul entered (Berakhot 62b): modesty (tzniut) is the protective garment of holiness. Because Saul guarded himself with supreme modesty, David recognized the divine anointing resting upon him and refrained from harming him, teaching that inward modesty shields a person from the counsel of the inclination even in moments of fierce testing.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 1:7: ‘God made the expanse, and it separated the water that was below the expanse from the water that was above the expanse. And it was so.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 1:7) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is Genesis 1:7: "And He separated between the waters below the firmament and the waters above the firmament, etc.", and this is the breadth between north and south— representing cold and heat, and as the...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Through that attribute the light reaches the lower heh, Knesses Yisrael. Sometimes He 'grants' the light and sometimes He 'lends' it. Hence the verse says 'is gracious and lends': on one occasion the illumination comes as a free gift from the Holy One; on another it is lent so that there may be an awakening from below, assisted by an awakening from above.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this underlies the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua (Rosh Hashanah 11a): Rabbi Eliezer held that the world was created in Tishrei, whereas Rabbi Yehoshua held that the world was created in Nisan. And their dispute centers on these verses: Rabbi Eliezer expounded: “And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree”—which month is it when the earth puts forth grasses and trees are laden with ripe fruit? You must say: this is Tishrei.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 5b: ‘In praise of that stringency, the Sages added that Rabbi Ḥama said that Rabbi Ḥanina said that Rabbi Yitzḥak said: One who places his bed facing north to south will be rewarded with male children, as it is stated: “And whose belly You fill with Your treasure [utzfunekha], who have sons in plenty and leave their abundance to their babies” (Psalms 17:14). This verse indicates that one who sets his bed facing north will be rewarded with sons in plenty, as north [tzafon] is etymologically similar to Your treasure [tzfunekha].’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 5b) to illuminate his teaching here (“and as the early masters explained regarding "one who places his bed between north and south" Berakhot 5b. And the boundary fence in this is the firmament of heaven. For envy is banished outside the world, as I wrote...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: "And he will have male children" (Berakhot 5b), as stated in chapter HaMapelet (Niddah 31a): "If a woman emits seed first, she gives birth to a male." The meaning is: "male" signifies that the spiritual offspring is worthy and consummate, and as written in Bava Batra (16b): "Praiseworthy is he whose children are males"; for in the generation of good deeds there are two distinct dimensions, matching what is taught in Shabbat (63a): "He who performs a mitzvah according to its true mandate (k'ma'amarah)," implying that there is an observance not fully aligned with its inner mandate.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 5:9
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And as brought in the Talmud (Berakhot 51a): “Ten things were stated regarding the cup of blessing, etc., and he places his eyes upon it.” 'Cup' points to the Kingdom of Heaven which has no eyes of its own, and man must draw eyes unto it through the holy service he performs; for all of man's labor is to elevate everything unto vision and conscious knowledge, to know Hashem Who sanctifies them.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 6:11: ‘The earth became corrupt before God; the earth was filled with lawlessness.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 6:11) to illuminate his teaching here (“for "the earth was filled with violence" Genesis 6:11; whereas desire is intrinsic to the inhabited world, only that it is evil toward Heaven, being banished outside the Levitical camp;”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And likewise: "they took them wives of all that they chose" (Genesis 6:2)— "and they took" represents lust, and "of all, etc."—from this sprouted envy, where this one coveted the portion of that one; and therefore they are termed "sons of God" in the plural. And in the words of our Sages they are named Uzza and Azael, both sharing the etymology of fierce boldness (azzut), audacity, and rebellion against their Maker; and 'El' signifies power, and this second one manifests his audacity through forceful violence.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 11:1–2
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: So too, because our father Avraham questioned: "Can it be that the world is without a ruler?" the Holy One said to him: "I am the Master of the universe" (Bereishit Rabbah 39:1). And the concept is: when Avraham our Father saw the Generation of the Flood who expanded themselves excessively, possessing no unity among them but robbery and violence, as written (Genesis 6:13): “for the earth is filled with violence”, the opposite of what Hashem established, Who created the world in lovingkindness, as written: “The world is built on lovingkindness”.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Pesachim 94a: ‘The Gemara explains: Rava holds like that statement which Rabba bar bar Ḥana said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: How far can an average person walk in a day? One can walk ten parasangs, which are forty mil. This is explained: From dawn until sunrise one can walk a distance of five mil; from sunset until the emergence of the stars one can walk another five mil. Therefore, it is found that the thickness of the firmament is one-sixth of the distance that the sun travels during the day. Between sunrise and sunset, the sun travels a distance of six thousand parasangs during the amount of time an average person can walk thirty mil. During the dawn and twilight periods in the morning and evening,…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:12, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Pesachim 94a) to illuminate his teaching here (“they stated in Pesachim 94a: "one-sixth of the world", for the six workdays represent active service, and Shabbat is Torah, as our Sages of blessed memory taught Yalkut Shimoni, Vayakhel 408:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Wherefore immediately following his circumcision the angels arrived to announce the birth of Isaac, Abraham being now prepared and capable of siring him. And I heard that the three angels who came filled the entire universe, for an angel measures one third of the cosmos as the Sages stated [in Chullin 91b: an angel spans two thousand parasangs, while the cosmos spans six thousand parasangs as written in Pesachim 94a], and the entire world was filled with holiness through the angels, the whole atmospheric space of the world being purged of defilement and external husks.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this explains Midrash Tanchuma (Ki Tisa 33): Why does Hashem perform “work” on Shabbat by blowing winds, lifting clouds, and sending rain? A parable of one who owns two adjoining courtyards, etc. The inner meaning is: for mortal man, extracting potential into actualization constitutes labor, transferring from one domain to another; whereas with the Blessed Name there is no division or change between potential and actual, all being unified as one before Him.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Leviticus 19:2: ‘Speak to the whole Israelite community and say to them:You shall be holy, for I, the ETERNAL your God, am holy.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:13, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Leviticus 19:2) to illuminate his teaching here (“and as it is written Leviticus 19:2: "You shall be holy"— meaning separated, bounded, and specifically for the reason "for I, Hashem, am holy." And as it is written Micah 6:8: "and to walk humbly"—”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For this reason superfluous bodily indulgences were forbidden by the commandment "You shall be holy" (Leviticus 19:2; see Ramban there) [and this is what is stated in Shabbat (31a): "'wisdom'—this refers to Seder Kodashim," where one must still remain holy and separated from worldly desires, as our Sages stated: wherever you find a fence against immorality you find holiness; and as I wrote elsewhere on Berakhot (10b): "'He is a holy man'—whence did she know this?"
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 44:10
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this principle we find likewise in trees and annual crops, which embody the mystery of male and female: annual crops are sown anew each year, which is in the aspect of female; while trees are planted once and yield fruit every year of themselves, the sap ascending, irrigating, and producing fruit, as brought in Rashi in Rosh Hashanah (12b), and this is in the mystery of male; therefore Hashem's commandment concerning fruit trees is (Leviticus 19:23–24).

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Micah 6:8: ‘“You have been told, O mortal, what is good,And what GOD requires of you:Only to do justiceAnd to love goodness,And to walk modestly with your God;’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:13, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Micah 6:8) to illuminate his teaching here (“And as it is written Micah 6:8: "and to walk humbly"— which refers precisely to erecting boundaries— "with your God." And as they stated in the chapter 'Bameh Madlikin' Shabbat 33b:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Except that in truth this is to his disparagement as noted above, for his entire intent was disgraceful. Nevertheless, in relation to Israel it yielded good, and Esther merited, as our Sages taught (ibid. 13b): “In reward for the modesty that she maintained, etc.,” and she absorbed the holy attribute of modesty, "to walk humbly with your God" (Micah 6:8), which likewise stems from this trait—to abide in concealment and not in overt revelation.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “Noah was a righteous man.” In Tanchuma (Nitzavim 1): This is what Scripture says (Proverbs 12:7): “The wicked are overthrown, and are not; but the house of the righteous shall stand” — whenever the Holy One scrutinizes the deeds of the wicked and overturns them, they have no remedy; He overturned the deeds of the Flood generation and they had no survival, as said: “and He blotted out all existence”; Israel, however, falls and rises, as said: “Rejoice not against me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall arise”; therefore it is said: “The wicked are overthrown and are not, but the house of the righteous shall stand.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 33b: ‘They said to him: Women will prove that dereliction in the study of Torah is not the cause, as they are not obligated to study Torah and, nevertheless, they contract askara. He answered them: They are punished because they cause their husbands to be idle from the study of Torah. They said to him: Gentiles will prove that this is not the cause, as they also contract askara even though they are not obligated to study Torah. He answered them: They are also punished because they cause Israel to be idle from the study of Torah. They said to him: Children will prove that this is not the cause, for they are not at all obligated to study Torah and they also suffer from askara. He answered them:…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:13, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 33b) to illuminate his teaching here (“And as they stated in the chapter 'Bameh Madlikin' Shabbat 33b: they instituted marketplaces so that everything be accessible, which is deeds of kindness, the opposite of envy, bridges”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 4:3 (§4)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this serves as testimony that Israel alone are the masters of Torah, bringing the utter destruction of Edom who usurped this claim. And the verdict against them is proclaimed: "Yet I loved Jacob, and I hated Esau" [Malachi 1:2–3]; for these are holy flesh and Hashem's assembly whose deeds are fundamentally good; whereas those, even when performing seemingly philanthropic deeds, act with disingenuous motives, as stated in Shabbat (33b) and Avodah Zarah (2b): they built bridges and bathhouses solely for their own selfish advantage.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: For behold, five stages exist in bringing potential into deed, ordered hierarchically: contemplation (hirhur), thought (machashavah), will (ratzon), action (ma'aseh), and speech (dibur). Even though outwardly action appears to be the final stage, in truth speech is the ultimate completion, as taught in Shabbat (33b): “Though kidneys advise, heart understands, and tongue articulates—the mouth concludes and completes”; and in Zohar Mikeitz (200a): “Thought is the inception of all, and word is the culmination of all.”

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 47a: ‘The Gemara recounts: Ravin and Abaye were traveling along the road on donkeys. Ravin’s donkey preceded Abaye’s and Ravin did not say to Abaye: Let the Master go first. Abaye said to himself: Ever since this one of the Sages, Ravin, ascended from the West, Eretz Yisrael, he has become arrogant. When they reached the door of the synagogue, Ravin said to Abaye: Let the Master enter first. Abaye said to him: Until now was I not Master? Why do you only begin deferring to me now but did not do so while we were traveling? Ravin said to him: Rabbi Yoḥanan said the following: One only defers to those greater than he at a doorway that has a mezuza, as only there is it appropriate to allow him to…’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:13, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Berakhot 47a) to illuminate his teaching here (“counteracting honor, as it is written Berakhot 47a: "We do not show honor in a bathhouse"— all for their own selfish needs, it amounts to nothing. And as they said in the chapter 'Hayah Notel' Sotah 22a:”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Ref: Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud:5 (§21)
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: By way of analogy: the Sadducees and the Samaritans, who profess belief in the Written Torah, and every commandment they observed they scrutinized meticulously, etc. (Berakhot 47b); yet they scrutinized according to their own flawed logic in the intent of the commandments; as by way of analogy: 'an eye for an eye' (Exodus 21:24) they expound as a literal physical eye, and according to their premise they imagine they uphold the Torah with all their might; while in truth through this they descend into the pit of destruction.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Noah was the first to accept the governance of Adonai—the sheath for Havayah—screening direct light so it flows gradually according to human merit; becoming disciplined in awe to mend the breach, partaking of worldly goods through moderation, composure, and derech eretz. The culmination was reached in Abraham: “From the day the world was created no one called God ‘Master’ (Adon) until Abraham came, saying: ‘O Lord God (Adonai Elohim), whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it’” (Berakhot 7b) —.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sotah 22a: ‘The Gemara asks: Is that so? But didn’t Rabbi Yoḥanan say: We learned the meaning of fear of sin from a maiden, and the significance of receiving divine reward from a widow. The meaning of fear of sin can be learned from a maiden, as Rabbi Yoḥanan heard a certain maiden who fell on her face in prayer, and she was saying: Master of the Universe, You created the Garden of Eden and You created Gehenna, You created the righteous and You created the wicked. May it be Your will that men shall not stumble because of me and consequently go to Gehenna.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:13, Rav Tzadok draws upon this talmudic and halakhic source (Sotah 22a) to illuminate his teaching here (“And as they said in the chapter 'Hayah Notel' Sotah 22a: a maiden who spends her time in fasting and prayer— a practitioner of divine service; a widow who wanders about to visit neighbors—”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: That is, because the Blessed Name does not desire that there exist in the world a creature who causes harm to another creature. And thus acted that pious man in Ta'anit 24a Rabbi Yosi of Yukrat who prayed that his daughter return to her dust so that men would not stumble into sin because of her; and so pleaded that maiden in Sotah 22a that men should not stumble through her beauty, as written in Shabbat 149b: "Anyone on whose account his fellow is punished, etc."
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And this is why he strikes him on the mouth, as it is taught (Shabbat 33b): “The mouth concludes and completes.” For through this strike whereby the light was forgotten, his spiritual form as an agent of free choice was completed, empowered to acquire the light through his own initiative now that the primordial light was concealed from him; and though his evil inclination entices him to act contrary to the divine Will, man through his righteous choice overcomes it to serve his Creator, earning the light on his own merit so that it is called “the toil of his own hands”—which is man's ultimate purpose.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Genesis 6:16: ‘Make an opening for daylight in the ark, and terminate it within a cubit of the top. Put the entrance to the ark in its side; make it with bottom, second, and third decks.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:13, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Genesis 6:16) to illuminate his teaching here (“And this is Genesis 6:16: "A window/illumination shall you make for the Ark"— Micah 7:8 "Though I sit in darkness, Hashem is a light unto me", that while he is occupied with the realm of practical actions, he should...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source clarifies the spiritual dynamic of Torah, character refinement, and divine service developed in this passage of Kometz HaMinchah.
Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is the intermediate level in the birth of Joseph the righteous, foundation of the world (Yesod Olam), which is the actualization of the sanctity of Yesod in this world in expansiveness, through whom this sanctity was clarified in practice through trials; there arose anew heavenly accusations from claims that there exist those who are not so, and that such exalted holiness is not yet worthy of being manifested in the world in practice within an individualized soul clothed in a physical body, for the foundation of the world to be drawn down and clothed in this world in deed within the seed of Jacob.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: The resolution of this matter is that the Blessed Name structured reality so it appears to creations that there is an empty void and interval separating His light from mortal perception; yet through dedicated divine service, man clarifies and reveals that His glory truly fills the entire universe. And if a person commits a transgression, heaven forbid, he creates a void and rupture from his own side, as stated in the Holy Zohar (Bereishit 6a; Tikkun 30, 73b): “One who enters into the void of the circle and the square”; and then the Blessed Name exposes the bare truth, as He showed in the generation of the Flood, that He has no need for created beings.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Micah 7:8: ‘Do not rejoice over me,O my enemy! Though I have fallen, I rise again;Though I sit in darkness, GOD is my light.’ Context and connection to Kometz HaMinchah: In Kometz HaMinchah 2:13, Rav Tzadok draws upon this scriptural verse (Micah 7:8) to illuminate his teaching here (“Micah 7:8 "Though I sit in darkness, Hashem is a light unto me", that while he is occupied with the realm of practical actions, he should not forget the internal service of the heart. Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: Meriting to cleave to the Tree of Life, named Noah as bringing rest to the world. Yet for his descendants he secured life only across the six thousand years, corresponding to the six seasons enumerated here. The essential constriction for God's glory began with Abraham onward, seen in Joseph taking the fifth part, teaching the integration of time through holy labor: “He who toiled on Friday shall eat on Shabbat” (Avodah Zarah 3a); this world being “the eve of Shabbat,” mirroring the years of abundance where man can imagine himself master to indulge at will.

And that is because 'priest' signifies a servant of Hashem, and because he recognized Avraham our Father as completely righteous, he did not comprehend why he risked his life to rescue Lot from whom the wicked neighbors of Jerusalem were destined to descend; wherefore he acted as a priest performing divine service, praying unto Hashem.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Sanhedrin 16b: ‘§ The mishna states that a city may be designated as an idolatrous city only in accordance with the ruling of the Great Sanhedrin, consisting of seventy-one judges. Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” This is what Scripture states (Psalms 92:1–2): “A psalm, a song for the Sabbath day: It is good to give thanks to the Lord and to sing praises to Your Name, Most High.” “Bereishit” (In the beginning) refers to the matter that the Blessed Name clarified and refined all the foundational elements, and this is encompassed within the word “Bereishit”; as we have seen that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, his entire holy labor was focused on the word “Bereishit,” refining and recombining the word “Bereishit” in seventy ways throughout the Holy Zohar and the Tikkunim.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 54a: ‘The mishna articulates a general principle: One is obligated to recite a blessing for the bad that befalls him just as he recites a blessing for the good that befalls him, as it is stated: “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5). Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: And this is termed "with all your heart"—with both your inclinations (Berakhot 54a), for a "tzadik" subdues his inclination, whereas this person introduces holiness even into the desires of the inclination; and then the Blessed Name, measure for measure, instills holiness into all that he does, and he merits to extract vast holiness specifically out of the evil inclination; and then he is termed "very good," which is superior to ordinary good; and regarding this it was said: "In the place where penitents stand, the wholly righteous cannot stand, etc." (Berakhot 34b).
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Ref: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 21:7–8
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And as brought in the Talmud (Berakhot 16b): “We do not call 'Fathers' except three,” meaning upon them Hashem set His seal that they are the foundation, beginning, and core, and whatever they fathered are offspring and branches, unable to equal the Patriarchs' virtues in totality. Therefore we bow at the opening of the blessing of the Patriarchs, hinting that they are the pillars and we desire to be integrated in their service of love and awe; and at 'Shield of Abraham' we bow a second time.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Berakhot 4a: ‘And so it says regarding Benayahu ben Yehoyada’s position as head of the Sanhedrin: “And Benayahu ben Yehoyada was over the Kereti and over the Peleti” (II Samuel 20:23). Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: For the rung of Solomon is that his deeds prosper exceedingly, seeing that all his achievements flow directly from Hashem's Will, fulfilling "the lip of truth shall be established forever"; whereas King David called himself "poor", fearing lest sin cause failure ("were it not that I believed", Berakhot 4a), never feeling self-assured; and the Holy One credited him in his own merit, his Holy Spirit and divine aid deriving from his own breath; whereas to them Heaven credited others' merit, all Holy Spirit after David deriving from his inheritance.
Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: And so was the matter here: after the Flood the World of Rectification was strengthened, built with greater durability and being. Therefore in the ten generations from Adam to Noah (Noah included) it is written “and he died”; while in the ten generations from Noah to Abraham “and he died” is not stated — because the first were remnants of the shattered worlds (the Kings of Edom, Zohar Naso 142a), where concerning each king it is written “and he reigned and died,” while regarding the last “and he died” is omitted, marking the inception of the World of Rectification (section 20).

Kisvei_Beis_Ishbitz_Radzin_Parallel_Tran: As written (Ezekiel 1:20): “the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels; whithersoever the spirit was to go, they went” — meaning they hold no independent volition of their own, but wherever Hashem directs them, there they nullify their will before the supreme Will. And in this physical world garments exist for all supernal realms, mirroring the divine pattern; and the fish of the sea allude to Atika Kadisha, being rooted in a light supremely close to the supreme Will, manifesting in this world in a form stripped of moral free choice.

Kisvei_Rav_Tzadok_Parallel_Translation: Wherefore the offering of the new meal-offering is designated "in your weeks" (Bamidbar 28:26); the counting of the preceding weeks being the catalyst for this new offering merited by Israel who count by the moon (Sukkah 29a), who are destined to be renewed like her (Sanhedrin 42a), attaining renewal after every concealment; and this counting brings about the sanctity of the festival, after having consecrated the preceding weeks through his count so that all his faculties are holy unto Hashem.

As it is said: “And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, herb yielding seed, and fruit tree”—which month is it when the earth puts forth grasses and trees are laden with fruit? You must say: this is Tishrei.

Primary_Source_Translation_And_Context: Shabbat 152a: ‘The Gemara relates: The Roman emperor said to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya: What is the reason you did not come to the House of Avidan?
